Throughout this section, we present the secret key variants, where the adversary has oracle access to a verification oracle 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗏𝗄\mathsf{Ver}_{\mathsf{vk}}. In Remark 3.8, we describe the corresponding public key variants, obtained by simply giving the adversary explicit access to 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk}.

Robustness requires that it is hard for an efficient adversary—even with access to both the watermarking oracle and the verification oracle—to produce a string ζ\zeta that contains a ℓ𝗋𝖻\ell_{\mathsf{rb}}-sized substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta which is Φ\Phi-close to one of the watermarked responses y←𝖶𝖺𝗍⁡(𝗌𝗄,x)y\leftarrow{\mathsf{Wat}}(\mathsf{sk},x) it observed, yet for which ζ\zeta fails to verify.

Definition 3.4 (Robustness).

For any closeness predicate Φ\Phi and any substring size ℓ𝗋𝖻=poly⁡(λ)\ell_{\mathsf{rb}}=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda), a watermarking scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖵𝖾𝗋)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},\mathsf{Ver}) is secret key (Φ,ℓ𝗋𝖻)(\Phi,\ell_{\mathsf{rb}})-robust if for any PPT algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputting ζ∈{0,1}∗\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{*},

Pr[(𝗏𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄,𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗏𝗄​(1λ):(∃ζ∗⪯ζ,(x,y)∈Π such that OPENΦ⁡(ζ∗,y)=1∧|ζ∗|=ℓ𝗋𝖻)∧𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=0]≤negl(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{vk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \zeta&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}},\mathsf{Ver}_{\mathsf{vk}}}(1^{\lambda})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\Big(\exists\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta,(x,y)\in\Pi\text{ such that }\\ \Phi(\zeta^{*},y)=1\wedge\;|\zeta^{*}|=\ell_{\mathsf{rb}}\Big)\\ \wedge\;\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=0\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi denotes the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

We include the substring requirement, |ζ∗|=ℓ𝗋𝖻|\zeta^{*}|=\ell_{\mathsf{rb}}, for two reasons. First, we cannot guarantee that the watermark is verifiable in arbitrarily small ζ\zeta, so this requirement imposes a lower bound on the size of ζ\zeta. Second, it allows us to capture adversaries who approximately copy a portion of their output, ζ∗\zeta^{*}, from the watermarked model, then insert arbitrary text around it. The substring size specifies exactly how much the text must be copied for the watermark to verify, regardless of the surrounding content.

Unforgeability complements robustness by requiring that it is hard for an efficient adversary to produce a string ζ\zeta that verifies as watermarked, but for which ζ\zeta contains no ℓ𝗎𝖿\ell_{\mathsf{uf}}-sized substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta that is Φ\Phi-close to any watermarked response yy observed by the adversary. Another interpretation of unforgeability is that if all ℓ𝗎𝖿\ell_{\mathsf{uf}}-sized substrings ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta are far from all of the watermarked responses yy seen by the adversary, then verification must fail.

Definition 3.5 (Unforgeability).

For any closeness predicate Φ\Phi and any substring size ℓ𝗎𝖿=poly⁡(λ)\ell_{\mathsf{uf}}=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda), a watermarking scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖵𝖾𝗋)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},\mathsf{Ver}) is secret key (Φ,ℓ𝗎𝖿)(\Phi,\ell_{\mathsf{uf}})-unforgeable if for any PPT algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputting ζ∈{0,1}∗\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{*},

Pr⁡[(𝗏𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄,𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗏𝗄​(1λ):𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=1∧¬(∃ζ∗⪯ζ,(x,y)∈Π such that OPENΦ⁡(ζ∗,y)=1∧|ζ∗|=ℓ𝗎𝖿)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{vk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \zeta&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}},\mathsf{Ver}_{\mathsf{vk}}}(1^{\lambda})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=1\\ \wedge\;\neg\Big(\exists\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta,(x,y)\in\Pi\text{ such that }\\ \Phi(\zeta^{*},y)=1\;\wedge\;|\zeta^{*}|=\ell_{\mathsf{uf}}\Big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi denotes the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

These definitions provide security for binary watermark verification. However, we may wish to go further and track the edits applied to content by recovering the original model outputs. Recoverable watermarking schemes provide exactly this capability. Robustness for a recoverable watermarking scheme requires that no efficient adversary can produce a string ζ\zeta containing a sufficiently long substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta that is Φ\Phi-close to some watermarked response yy, yet for which the recovery algorithm does not recover a substring of that response ξ⪯y\xi\preceq y. This recovered substring ξ\xi must also be similar to the copied ζ∗\zeta^{*} in size (up to an allowed loss).

Definition 3.6 (Robust recoverability).

For any closeness predicate Φ\Phi, substring size ℓ𝗋𝖾𝖼=poly⁡(λ)\ell_{\mathsf{rec}}=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda), and loss size ℓ𝗅𝗈𝗌𝗌=poly⁡(λ)\ell_{\mathsf{loss}}=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda), a recoverable watermarking scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) is secret key (Φ,ℓ𝗋𝖾𝖼,ℓ𝗅𝗈𝗌𝗌)(\Phi,\ell_{\mathsf{rec}},\ell_{\mathsf{loss}})-robust if for any PPT algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputting ζ∈{0,1}∗\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{*},

Pr⁡[(𝗏𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄,𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗏𝗄​(1λ)ℒ←𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ):(∃ζ∗⪯ζ,(x,y)∈Π such that OPENΦ⁡(ζ∗,y)=1∧|ζ∗|≥ℓ𝗋𝖾𝖼)∧ℒ​ does not contain a(|ζ∗|−ℓ𝗅𝗈𝗌𝗌)​-sized substring of ​y]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{vk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \zeta&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}},{\mathsf{Rec}}_{\mathsf{vk}}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \mathcal{L}&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\Big(\exists\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta,(x,y)\in\Pi\text{ such that }\\ \Phi(\zeta^{*},y)=1\;\wedge\;|\zeta^{*}|\geq\ell_{\mathsf{rec}}\Big)\;\wedge\\ \mathcal{L}\text{ does not contain a}\\ (|\zeta^{*}|-\ell_{\mathsf{loss}})\text{-sized substring of }y\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi denotes the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

To ensure that recoveries are reliable, it is natural to additionally require that any recovered text truly originates from the model. This requirement is especially important in applications where recovered substrings are used for fine-grained attribution. One could rely on standard unforgeability, which guarantees that whenever the recovered list 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ){\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta) contains a string ξ\xi, there exists some observed response yy that is close to a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta. However, this does not ensure that the recovery ξ\xi itself was genuinely observed by the adversary. Instead, we require unforgeable recoverability: no efficient adversary can produce text ζ\zeta such that 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ){\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta) recovers a string ξ\xi which is either too small, or is not a substring of any response yy that was approximately copied by the adversary.

Definition 3.7 (Unforgeable recoverability).

For any closeness predicate Φ\Phi and any substring size ℓ𝗋𝖾𝖼=poly⁡(λ)\ell_{\mathsf{rec}}=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda), a recoverable watermarking scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) is secret key (Φ,ℓ𝗋𝖾𝖼)(\Phi,\ell_{\mathsf{rec}})-unforgeable if for any PPT algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputting ζ∈{0,1}∗\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{*},

Pr⁡[(𝗏𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄,𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗏𝗄​(1λ):∃ξ∈𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)​ such that ​(|ξ|<ℓ𝗋𝖾𝖼)∨¬(∃ζ∗⪯ζ,(x,y)∈Π withOPENΦ⁡(ζ∗,y)=1∧|ζ∗|=|ξ|∧ξ⪯y)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{vk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \zeta&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}},{\mathsf{Rec}}_{\mathsf{vk}}}(1^{\lambda})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\exists\xi\in{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)\text{ such that }\Big(|\xi|<\ell_{\mathsf{rec}}\big)\\ \vee\;\neg\Big(\exists\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta,(x,y)\in\Pi\text{ with}\\ \Phi(\zeta^{*},y)=1\wedge\;|\zeta^{*}|=|\xi|\;\wedge\;\xi\preceq y\Big)\\ \end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi denotes the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

Remark 3.8.

We presented the secret key variants of all our definitions, where the attacker receives oracle access to both 𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}} and 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗏𝗄\mathsf{Ver}_{\mathsf{vk}}. We also consider the corresponding public key variants, which are identical except that the attacker additionally receives the full verification key 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} (rather than only black-box access to the verification oracle).

Remark 3.9.

We do not include a loss term ℓ𝗅𝗈𝗌𝗌\ell_{\mathsf{loss}} in the definition of unforgeable recoverability, because our construction guarantees the existence of a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta that has exactly the same length as the recovered string.

Remark 3.10.

We define standard robustness to consider fixed-size substrings |ζ∗|=ℓ𝗋𝖻|\zeta^{*}|=\ell_{\mathsf{rb}}, but allow variable-size substrings |ζ∗|≥ℓ𝗋𝖾𝖼|\zeta^{*}|\geq\ell_{\mathsf{rec}} for recoverable robustness. One could additionally define a dynamic version of standard robustness, in which verification succeeds whenever there exists a close substring ζ∗\zeta^{*} with |ζ∗|≥ℓ𝗋𝖻|\zeta^{*}|\geq\ell_{\mathsf{rb}}. Our construction in fact satisfies this property. However, we include it explicitly only in the definition of recoverability for two reasons:

  1. 1.

    It is meaningful there, as it allows us to capture that the size of the recovered output ξ∈ℒ\xi\in\mathcal{L} scales with the size of the approximate copy ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta.

  2. 2.

    Standard robustness typically implies this behavior implicitly. In particular, consider (Φ,ℓrb)(\Phi,\ell_{\mathrm{rb}})-robustness for a predicate Φ\Phi satisfying the following: for any ζ∈{0,1}∗\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{*} with |ζ|≥ℓ𝗋𝖻|\zeta|\geq\ell_{\mathsf{rb}},

    Φ⁡(ζ,y)=1⟹∃ζ∗⪯ζ​ with ​|ζ∗|=ℓ𝗋𝖻​ and ​Φ​(ζ∗,y)=1,\Phi(\zeta,y)=1\implies\exists\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta\text{ with }|\zeta^{*}|=\ell_{\mathsf{rb}}\text{ and }\Phi(\zeta^{*},y)=1\;,

    Under this condition, standard robustness implies the dynamic notion of robustness. If ζ\zeta contains a substring ζ′\zeta^{\prime} with |ζ′|>ℓ𝗋𝖻|\zeta^{\prime}|>\ell_{\mathsf{rb}} that is Φ\Phi-close to a response yy, then by the above property there exists a further substring ζ∗⪯ζ′⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta^{\prime}\preceq\zeta of size exactly ℓ𝗋𝖻\ell_{\mathsf{rb}} that is also Φ\Phi-close to yy. (Φ,ℓ𝗋𝖻)(\Phi,\ell_{\mathsf{rb}})-robustness then guarantees that verification succeeds on ζ\zeta.

4 Preliminaries

Digital signatures.

We recall the definition of (non-robust) digital signature schemes. Digital signature schemes allow a signer to associate a message with their publicly-verifiable signature. Parties without the signing key cannot forge valid signatures on messages that the signer has not signed. Here, we define digital signatures with strong unforgeability [8]. While standard unforgeability only prevents a forger from creating a valid signature for a new message, strong unforgeability goes further: it prevents the forger from producing a new valid signature, even for a message whose signature it has already seen.

Definition 4.1 (Digital signature scheme).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be the message size, and k=poly⁡(λ)k=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be the signature size. A digital signature scheme is a triple (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖵𝖾𝗋)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},\mathsf{Ver}) of PPT algorithms satisfying,

  • •

    𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ):{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}): outputs a pair of public and secret keys (𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk}).

  • •

    𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇⁡(𝗌𝗄,y):{\mathsf{Sign}}(\mathsf{sk},y): takes in the secret key 𝗌𝗄\mathsf{sk} and a message y∈{0,1}ny\in\{0,1\}^{n} and outputs a signature σ∈{0,1}k\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{k}.

  • •

    𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ):\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma): takes in the public key 𝗉𝗄\mathsf{pk}, a string ζ∈{0,1}n\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{n}, and a signature σ∈{0,1}k\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{k} and outputs a binary decision b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}.

Correctness: For any y∈{0,1}ny\in\{0,1\}^{n},

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)σ←𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇⁡(𝗌𝗄,y):𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗉𝗄,y,σ)=1]=1,\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \sigma&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sign}}(\mathsf{sk},y)\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{pk},y,\sigma)=1\end{array}\right]=1\;,

Strong unforgeability: For any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(ζ,σ)←𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄​(𝗉𝗄):(𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=1)∧((ζ,σ)∉Π)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (\zeta,\sigma)&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{pk})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\Big(\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)=1\Big)\;\wedge\;\Big((\zeta,\sigma)\notin\Pi\Big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi is the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

Collision resistant hash.

The sharp sketch construction of Dodis et al. [16] and property-preserving hash construction of Holmgren et al. [26] rely on the existence of collision resistant hash functions (CRHFs). We recall their definition here.

Definition 4.2 (Collision resistant hash).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter and let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) and k=poly⁡(λ)k=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be such that k≤nk\leq n. A collision resistant hash family (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,{ℋλ})({\mathsf{Sample}},\{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\}) consists of an efficient algorithm h←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)h\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda}) that samples a hash function h∈ℋλh\in\mathcal{H}_{\lambda} with h:{0,1}n→{0,1}kh:\{0,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\{0,1\}^{k}. We require,

Efficiency: Given x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} and h←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)h\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda}), the function h⁡(x)h(x) can be computed in time poly⁡(λ)\mathrm{poly}(\lambda).

Collision-resistance: For any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr⁡[h←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)(x,x′)←𝒜⁡(1λ,h):h⁡(x)=h⁡(x′)∧(x≠x′)]≤negl⁡(λ).\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}h&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (x,x^{\prime})&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(1^{\lambda},h)\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}h(x)=h(x^{\prime})\\ \wedge\;(x\neq x^{\prime})\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;.

Pseudorandom codes.

Pseudorandom codes (PRCs) are error-correcting codes whose codewords are indistinguishable from random binary vectors [14]. We use ideal security (defined by Alrabiah et al. [4]), which means that even an adversary with oracle access to the encoder and decoder cannot distinguish between a PRC scheme and an “ideal” random code scheme, whose codewords are uniformly random and decoder simply responds with exact proximity queries to the underlying transcript. Ideal security thus captures both the pseudorandomness and robustness properties that PRCs are designed to achieve.

PRC encoding and decoding keys.

In the PRC literature, the PRC encoding and decoding keys are often referred to as “public” and “secret” keys, respectively. However, in the watermarking setting, these roles are reversed: encoding is performed by the model provider, who holds the secret watermark key, while decoding is performed by users, who hold the public key and wish to verify the watermark. To avoid confusion, we refer to the PRC keys simply as the encoding and decoding keys, denoted 𝖾𝗄\mathsf{ek} and 𝖽𝗄\mathsf{dk}, respectively.

Definition 4.3 (Pseudorandom codes).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be a security parameter, k=p​o​l​y​(λ)k=poly(\lambda) be the message size, and n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be the block size. A PRC is a triple (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗇𝖼,𝖣𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Enc}},{\mathsf{Dec}}) of PPT algorithms satisfying,

  • •

    𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ):{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}): outputs encoding and decoding keys (𝖾𝗄,𝖽𝗄)(\mathsf{ek},\mathsf{dk}).

  • •

    𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝖾𝗄,σ):{\mathsf{Enc}}(\mathsf{ek},\sigma): takes in the encoding key 𝖾𝗄\mathsf{ek} and a message σ∈{0,1}k\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{k} and outputs a codeword y∈{0,1}ny\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

  • •

    𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝖽𝗄,ξ):{\mathsf{Dec}}(\mathsf{dk},\xi): takes in the decoding key 𝖽𝗄\mathsf{dk} and a string ξ∈{0,1}n\xi\in\{0,1\}^{n} and outputs message or decoding failure σ∈{0,1}k∪{⟂}\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{k}\cup\{\perp\}.

The information rate of the PRC is kn\frac{k}{n}.

Ideal security captures the core properties that PRCs are designed to satisfy. It asserts that no PPT adversary can distinguish between a real-world interaction with the PRC and an ideal-world interaction. In the real world, the adversary interacts with the PRC encoder and decoder via oracle access. In the ideal world, the adversary receives a fresh uniformly random string for each encoding query, and the decoder maintains a complete transcript of all past encodings, decoding only those strings that are sufficiently close to previously generated ones. This notion thus captures both pseudorandomness and robustness within a single definition. It is formalized through two security games, 𝒢\mathcal{G} and 𝒢𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{ideal}}.

𝒢λ​(𝒜)\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}(\mathcal{A}):

  1. 1.

    The challenger samples (𝖾𝗄,𝖽𝗄)←𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(\mathsf{ek},\mathsf{dk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}).

  2. 2.

    The adversary makes encoding and decoding queries.

    • •

      For each encoding query σ\sigma, the challenger responds with y←y\leftarrow 𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝖾𝗄CLOSE,{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Enc}}(\mathsf{ek}, OPENσ)\sigma).

    • •

      For each decoding query ξ\xi, the challenger responds with σ′←\sigma^{\prime}\leftarrow 𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝖽𝗄CLOSE,{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}(\mathsf{dk}, OPENξ)\xi).

  3. 3.

    The adversary returns a decision bit b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}.

𝒢δ,λ𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅​(𝒜)\mathcal{G}^{{\mathsf{ideal}}}_{\delta,\lambda}(\mathcal{A}):

  1. 1.

    The challenger initializes a transcript Π=∅\Pi=\emptyset.

  2. 2.

    The adversary makes encoding and decoding queries.

    • •

      For each encoding query σ\sigma, the challenger responds with a fresh random codeword y←{0,1}ny\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{n} and adds the entry (σ,y)(\sigma,y) to the transcript Π\Pi.

    • •

      For each decoding query ξ\xi, the challenger responds with a random message σ\sigma satisfying (σ,y)∈Π(\sigma,y)\in\Pi for some yy such that 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ​(y,ξ)=1{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}(y,\xi)=1. If no such σ\sigma exists, then the challenger responds with ⟂\perp.

  3. 3.

    The adversary returns a decision bit b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}.

Definition 4.4 (Ideal security).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter and δ∈(0,12)\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{2}) be the error-rate. A pseudorandom code (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗇𝖼,𝖣𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Enc}},{\mathsf{Dec}}) is ideal with error-rate δ\delta if, for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

|Pr[𝒢λ(𝒜)=1]−Pr[𝒢δ,λ𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅(𝒜)=1]|≤negl(λ).\left|\Pr\big[\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}(\mathcal{A})=1\big]-\Pr\big[\mathcal{G}^{{\mathsf{ideal}}}_{\delta,\lambda}(\mathcal{A})=1\big]\right|\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;.

Alrabiah et al. [4] construct ideal pseudorandom codes with constant error rate δ∈(0,14)\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{4}) while achieving a constant information rate ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), assuming the subexponential hardness of the exact learning parity with noise problem (LPN) [28].

Theorem 4.5 ([4, Corollary 5]).

Assume the subexponential hardness of exact LPN [4, Assumption 1]. For any constant δ∈(0,14)\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{4}), there exists a constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) such that there exists an ideal PRC with error-rate δ\delta and information rate ρ+o⁡(1)\rho+o(1).

4.1 Property-preserving hash

Property preserving hash functions (PPHs) [11] allow efficient computation of a predicate Φ\Phi on two strings using only their compressed hashes, even when those inputs are chosen adversarially with full knowledge of the hash.

Definition 4.6 (Property-preserving hash).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, let Φ\Phi be any predicate, and let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) and k=poly⁡(λ)k=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) with k≤nk\leq n be the input and hash size respectively. A PPH scheme for Φ\Phi is a triple of PPT algorithms (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁,𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅)({\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Hash}},{\mathsf{Eval}}) satisfying

  • •

    𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ):{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda}): samples a hash function hh from the family of functions ℋλ\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}.

  • •

    𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(h,x):{\mathsf{Hash}}(h,x): takes in the hash description hh and a string x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} and outputs a hash z∈{0,1}kz\in\{0,1\}^{k}.

  • •

    𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,z,z′):{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,z,z^{\prime}): takes in the hash description hh and strings z,z′∈{0,1}kz,z^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{k} and outputs an evaluation b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}.

Direct-access robustness: For any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr[h←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)(x,x′)←𝒜⁡(1λ,h):𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅(h,h(x),h(x′))≠Φ(x,x′)]≤negl(λ).\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}h&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (x,x^{\prime})&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(1^{\lambda},h)\end{array}:{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),h(x^{\prime}))\neq\mathrm{\Phi}(x,x^{\prime})\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;.

We use the notation h⁡(x):=𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(h,x)h(x):={\mathsf{Hash}}(h,x).

Prior works [20, 19, 26] have constructed PPHs for the Hamming predicate 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}. In particular, assuming the existence of a special type of homomorphic CRHF, the construction of Holmgren et al. [26] achieves constant-factor compression of the input when the error rate is constant.

Theorem 4.7 ([26, Corollary 6.7]).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) denote the input size. Suppose there exists a homomorphic CRHF with output size ℓ=ℓ⁡(λ)\ell=\ell(\lambda) that is collision-resistant over {−1,0,1}n\{-1,0,1\}^{n} [26, Definition 6.1]. Then, for any constants δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and ρ>H3𝖡𝖹​(δ)⋅log2⁡3\rho>H_{3}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta)\cdot\log_{2}3, where H3𝖡𝖹​(⋅)H_{3}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\cdot) refers to the Blokh-Zyablov bound [26, Fact 2.12], there exists a PPH for 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta} with hash size ρ⋅n+ℓ\rho\cdot n+\ell.

Remark 4.8 (Blokh-Zyablov).

The Blokh-Zyablov bound [9] is what best known constructions of efficiently list-decodable codes achieve [25]. It is a longstanding open problem in coding theory to match the Hamming bound H⁡(δ)H(\delta) with efficient codes. Note that log⁡(nδ​n)=n​H​(δ)+o⁡(n)\log\binom{n}{\delta n}=nH(\delta)+o(n).

Remark 4.9.

Theorem 4.7 relies on a specialized form of homomorphic CRHF, which can be constructed under either the shortest integer solution (SIS) assumption or the discrete logarithm assumption. Later, we instantiate a slightly weaker hash family that relies on standard CRHFs, but still suffices for our purposes (Theorem 5.6).

4.2 Block steganography

We use steganography as a tool in our watermarking constructions. Steganography is similar to watermarking but differs in three key respects. First, a steganography scheme enables messages to be robustly embedded in and decoded from generated text, rather than allowing only binary verification. Second, we only require correctness and robustness from steganography schemes, with no guarantees on soundness, unforgeability, or recoverability (i.e., no bound on false positives). Third, we consider block steganography, which produces a single, size nn block per invocation, whereas a full watermarking scheme generates an entire response, which could be arbitrarily long. This distinction is not significant: as shown below, a block-steganography scheme can be used to autoregressively generate a full response. The block interface is simply more convenient for later constructions.

Definition 4.10 (Block steganography).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, k=p​o​l​y​(λ)k=poly(\lambda) be the message size, and n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be the block size. A block steganography scheme for a language model QQ and token set {0,1}\{0,1\} is a tuple of polynomial time algorithms (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}) satisfying,

  • •

    𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ):{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}): takes in a security parameter λ\lambda and outputs verification and secret keys (𝗏𝗄,𝗌𝗄)(\mathsf{vk},\mathsf{sk}).

  • •

    𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽⁡(𝗌𝗄,π,m):{\mathsf{Embed}}(\mathsf{sk},\pi,m): takes in the secret key 𝗌𝗄\mathsf{sk}, a context π∈{0,1}∗\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}, and a message m∈{0,1}km\in\{0,1\}^{k} and outputs a block y∈{0,1}ny\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

  • •

    𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ):{\mathsf{Dec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta): takes in the verification key 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk} and input text ζ∈{0,1}n\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{n} and outputs a decoded message or a failure symbol m∈{0,1}k∪{⟂}m\in\{0,1\}^{k}\cup\{\perp\}.

Undetectability For every PPT distinguisher 𝒜\mathcal{A},

|Pr(𝗏𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)⁡[𝒜Q,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄​(1λ)=1]−Pr⁡[𝒜Q,Q¯n​(1λ)=1]|≤negl⁡(λ),\left|\Pr_{(\mathsf{vk},\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})}\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}\mathcal{A}^{Q,{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(1^{\lambda})=1\end{array}\right]-\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}\mathcal{A}^{Q,{\overline{Q}}_{n}}(1^{\lambda})=1\end{array}\right]\right|\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where both 𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}} and Q¯n{\overline{Q}}_{n} take in contexts π∈{0,1}∗\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*} and message m∈{0,1}km\in\{0,1\}^{k} as input, but Q¯n{\overline{Q}}_{n} ignores the message: Q¯n​(π,m):=Q¯n​(π){\overline{Q}}_{n}(\pi,m):={\overline{Q}}_{n}(\pi).

Robustness for block steganography is similar to robustness for watermarking, but allows decoding a message mm from an input ζ\zeta that is close to an embedding yy of that message.

Definition 4.11 (Block Robustness).

For any closeness predicate Φ\Phi, a block steganography scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}) with block size n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) is secret-key Φ\Phi-robust if for any PPT algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputting ζ∈{0,1}n\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{n},

Pr⁡[(𝗏𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)ζ←𝒜𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄,𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗏𝗄​(1λ):(∃(π,m,y)∈Π​ such thatCLOSEOPENΦ⁡(ζ,y)=1∧𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)≠m)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{vk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \zeta&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}},{\mathsf{Dec}}_{\mathsf{vk}}}(1^{\lambda})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\Big(\exists(\pi,m,y)\in\Pi\text{ such that}\\ \Phi(\zeta,y)=1\wedge\;{\mathsf{Dec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)\neq m\Big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi denotes the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

Remark 4.12.

Public-key Φ\Phi-robustness for block steganography is defined identically to the secret key variant, except the adversary receives the verification key 𝗏𝗄\mathsf{vk}.

Robust watermarking from block steganography.

Many existing watermarking schemes are explicitly or implicitly based on block steganography [14, 22, 17]. Below, we describe a simple watermarking scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍¯,𝖵𝖾𝗋¯)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\overline{{\mathsf{Wat}}}},{\overline{\mathsf{Ver}}}) that uses a steganography scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}) in an autoregressive manner, embedding arbitrary messages (e.g., the message 11) until a special 𝖽𝗈𝗇𝖾{\mathsf{done}} token signals that the model should output the string. While this scheme guarantees robustness, it does not provide unforgeability or recoverability, which are the focus of our construction in Section 6.1.

Here, we use the shorthand yt[<𝖽𝗈𝗇𝖾]y_{t}[<{\mathsf{done}}] to denote the substring of yty_{t} preceding the 𝖽𝗈𝗇𝖾{\mathsf{done}} token. The verification algorithm then examines every substring of size nn in its input ζ\zeta, and accepts if any of them decode to a message other than ⟂\perp.

In this construction, each block yty_{t} of a response y←𝖶𝖺𝗍¯​(𝗌𝗄,x)y\leftarrow{\overline{{\mathsf{Wat}}}}(\mathsf{sk},x) is generated as an embedding yt←𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽⁡(𝗌𝗄,π,1)y_{t}\leftarrow{\mathsf{Embed}}(\mathsf{sk},\pi,1). Consequently, in 𝖵𝖾𝗋¯​(𝗏𝗄,ζ){\overline{\mathsf{Ver}}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta), as long as the input ζ\zeta contains an nn-bit substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta that is Φ\Phi-close to some block yty_{t} of a response yy, the decoder 𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗){\mathsf{Dec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*}) outputs 11 except with negligible probability. This, in turn, ensures that 𝖵𝖾𝗋¯​(𝗏𝗄,ζ){\overline{\mathsf{Ver}}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta) also outputs 11. Recall that this condition is captured exactly by the predicate 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]​(ζ∗,y)\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n](\zeta^{*},y) (Definition 3.2), which, given ζ∗\zeta^{*} of size nn, outputs 1 iff it is Φ\Phi-close to a block of yy. We formalize this guarantee in Fact 4.13.

Fact 4.13.

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be any block size, Φ\Phi be any closeness predicate, and QQ be any language model. If (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}) is a block size nn steganography scheme for QQ with (secret or public key) Φ\Phi-robustness, then the watermarking scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍¯,𝖵𝖾𝗋¯)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\overline{{\mathsf{Wat}}}},{\overline{\mathsf{Ver}}}) for QQ satisfies (secret or public key) (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],n)-robustness.

Proof.

Undetectability follows immediately from the undetectability of the underlying steganography scheme. We now prove robustness for the secret key case; the public key version is analogous.

Fix a PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} and a security parameter λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N}. Let (𝗏𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(\mathsf{vk},\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}), let ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍¯𝗌𝗄,𝖵𝖾𝗋¯𝗏𝗄​(1λ)\zeta\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\overline{{\mathsf{Wat}}}}_{\mathsf{sk}},{\overline{\mathsf{Ver}}}_{\mathsf{vk}}}(1^{\lambda}), and let Π\Pi denote the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍¯𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\overline{{\mathsf{Wat}}}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}). Assume, toward contradiction, that there exists a polynomial q:ℕ→ℕq:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} such that

Pr[(∃ζ∗⪯ζ,(x,y)∈Π such that 𝖤𝖡𝖢[Φ,n](ζ∗,y)=1∧|ζ∗|=n)∧𝖵𝖾𝗋¯​(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=0]≥1/q(λ).\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}\big(\exists\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta,(x,y)\in\Pi\text{ such that }\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n](\zeta^{*},y)=1\wedge\;|\zeta^{*}|=n\big)\\ \wedge\;{\overline{\mathsf{Ver}}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=0\end{array}\right]\geq 1/q(\lambda)\;.

Whenever the above event occurs, the predicate 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]​(ζ∗,y)=1\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n](\zeta^{*},y)=1, with |ζ∗|=n|\zeta^{*}|=n, guarantees the existence of a block index t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} for which

Φ⁡(ζ∗,yt)=1.\Phi(\zeta^{*},y_{t})=1\;.

Because each block yty_{t} is produced by 𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}} during 𝒜\mathcal{A}’s interaction with 𝖶𝖺𝗍¯𝗌𝗄{\overline{{\mathsf{Wat}}}}_{\mathsf{sk}}, we have

(x,y)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍¯𝗌𝗄)⇒((π=(x,y1,…,yt−1),m=1),yt)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄).(x,y)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\overline{{\mathsf{Wat}}}}_{\mathsf{sk}}})\;\Rightarrow\;\Big((\pi=(x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{t-1}),\,m=1),\,y_{t}\Big)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}}})\;.

Yet in the same event, we also have 𝖵𝖾𝗋¯​(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=0{\overline{\mathsf{Ver}}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=0, which implies 𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗)=⟂{\mathsf{Dec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*})=\perp, since failed verification guarantees that every nn-bit substring of ζ\zeta decodes to ⟂\perp. Consequently, there exists an adversary ℬ\mathcal{B} that simulates 𝒜\mathcal{A} and outputs the substring ζ∗\zeta^{*}, which is Φ\Phi-close to an embedding block yty_{t} but fails to decode with probability at least 1/q⁡(λ)1/q(\lambda). This violates the Φ\Phi-block robustness of the underlying steganography scheme, yielding a contradiction. ∎

Block steganography instantiations.

We present existing constructions for both secret and public key robust block steganography schemes for language models with sufficiently high entropy.

Secret key block steganography from PRCs.

For the secret key setting, recall PRCs, which closely resemble block steganography schemes for the uniform language model (e.g., Q⁡(π)=1/2Q(\pi)=1/2 for all π∈{0,1}∗\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}). Christ and Gunn [14] showed that PRCs can be used to build a robust watermarking scheme. However, their construction leverages standard PRCs, which achieve a weaker form of robustness, where the robustness adversary is modeled as an error channel acting independently of the encoding and decoding keys. By plugging ideal PRCs [4] (as in Definition 4.4) into their construction, we essentially obtain the adaptive guarantee that we require.

A subtlety is that ideal PRCs guarantee that an input ξ\xi decodes to a random message mm whose encoding yy is close to ξ\xi, rather than the unique message mm as required in block steganography. We show that this distinction is harmless: due to pseudorandomness, no efficient adversary can find any ξ\xi that is simultaneously close to the encodings of two distinct messages.

Theorem 4.14 (Secret-key block steganography from ideal PRC [14, 4]).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) with n≥λn\geq\lambda be any block size, and let QQ be any language model with min-entropy rate at least a constant. That is, there exists a constant ϵ∈(0,14)\epsilon\in(0,\frac{1}{4}) such that

∀π∈{0,1}∗,y←Q¯ℓ​(π)​ satisfies ​H∞​(y)≥4​(12−ϵ)​n\forall\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*},y\leftarrow{\overline{Q}}_{\ell}(\pi)\text{ satisfies }H_{\infty}(y)\geq 4\Big(\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon}\Big)n

If there exists an ideal pseudorandom code with constant information rate ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and constant error rate δ∈(0,14)\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{4}), then there exists a block size nn secret key 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ−ϵ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta-\epsilon}-robust steganography scheme for QQ with message size k=ρ​nk=\rho n.

Proof.

Let 𝖯𝖱𝖢=(𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗇𝖼,𝖣𝖾𝖼){\mathsf{PRC}}=({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Enc}},{\mathsf{Dec}}) be a block size nn ideal PRC, assumed to exist in the theorem. We define 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀=(𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼){\mathsf{Steg}}=({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}), which mirrors the watermarking scheme of [14] but allows embedding messages and only outputs nn-sized blocks.

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ):{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}): samples encoding and decoding keys (𝖾𝗄,𝖽𝗄)←𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(\mathsf{ek},\mathsf{dk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}) and outputs (𝗏𝗄=𝖽𝗄,𝗌𝗄=𝖾𝗄)(\mathsf{vk}=\mathsf{dk},\mathsf{sk}=\mathsf{ek}).

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽⁡(𝗌𝗄,π,m){\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Embed}}(\mathsf{sk},\pi,m): encodes the message c←𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝗌𝗄,m)c\leftarrow{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Enc}}(\mathsf{sk},m) and then samples each bit of the response block y∈{0,1}ny\in\{0,1\}^{n} as

    y⁡[i]←𝖡𝖾𝗋⁡(pi−(−1)c⁡[i]⋅min⁡{pi,1−pi}),∀i∈[n],y[i]\leftarrow{\mathsf{Ber}}\Big(p_{i}-(-1)^{c[i]}\cdot\min\{p_{i},1-p_{i}\}\Big),\quad\forall i\in[n],

    where pi=Q(π,y[1:i])p_{i}=Q(\pi,y[1:i]) is the probability that the ii-th bit should be 11 under QQ. Then outputs yy.

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ∈{0,1}n){\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{n}) outputs m′←𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)m^{\prime}\leftarrow{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta).

Undetectability follows from pseudorandomness of 𝖯𝖱𝖢{\mathsf{PRC}} [14, Lemma 19]. For robustness fix λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} and a PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and let (𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖾𝗄,𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖽𝗄)←𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ)({\mathsf{PRC}}.\mathsf{ek},{\mathsf{PRC}}.\mathsf{dk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}) and ζ←𝒜𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄,𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗏𝗄​(1λ)\zeta\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}},{\mathsf{Dec}}_{\mathsf{vk}}}(1^{\lambda}). We will show that 𝒜\mathcal{A} cannot break the Φ\Phi-block robustness of 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}}.

We move to a hybrid in which the oracles 𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}} and 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗏𝗄{\mathsf{Dec}}_{\mathsf{vk}} are implemented using 𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Enc}}^{{\mathsf{ideal}}} and 𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}^{{\mathsf{ideal}}} respectively (the oracles given in the ideal PRC game 4, 𝒢λ,δ𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅​(𝒜)\mathcal{G}^{{\mathsf{ideal}}}_{\lambda,\delta}(\mathcal{A})). By the ideal security of 𝖯𝖱𝖢{\mathsf{PRC}}, this hybrid is computationally indistinguishable to 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Now consider the event that ζ\zeta is 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ−ϵ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta-\epsilon}-close to some block y∈{0,1}ny\in\{0,1\}^{n} for which

(π,m,y)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝗌𝗄).(\pi,m,y)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Embed}}_{\mathsf{sk}}})\;.

We will show that ζ\zeta decodes to mm with overwhelming probability. Since QQ has entropy rate at least a constant, every response yy has high empirical entropy as in [14, Definition 7]. From [14, Lemma 21], yy must therefore be 𝖧𝖺𝗆ϵ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\epsilon}-close to the PRC codeword cc used to sample it with all but negligible probability. That is, with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda), there exists a codeword c∈{0,1}nc\in\{0,1\}^{n} such that

(m,c)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅)​ and ​𝖧𝖺𝗆ϵ​(y,c)=1.(m,c)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Enc}}^{{\mathsf{ideal}}}})\text{ and }{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\epsilon}(y,c)=1\;. (1)

By the triangle inequality, ζ\zeta is 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}-close to cc. We want to argue that the ideal decoder will therefore decode ζ\zeta to the corresponding message mm. However, the ideal decoder only guarantees decoding to a random message satisfying 1. We now show that mm is, with overwhelming probability, the unique such message, which will conclude the argument.

Since 𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Enc}}^{{\mathsf{ideal}}} generates a fresh random codeword for each input, all codewords in the transcript are, with overwhelming probability, pairwise at a Hamming distance greater than 2​δ​n2\delta n. Formally, let

C={c:∃m′​ with ​(m′,c)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖺𝗅)}.C\;=\;\{\,c:\exists m^{\prime}\text{ with }(m^{\prime},c)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Enc}}^{{\mathsf{ideal}}}})\,\}.

By Lemma 4.15 and the fact that codewords from the ideal encoder are uniformly random strings, the probability that any two distinct c,c′∈Cc,c^{\prime}\in C satisfy

𝖧𝖺𝗆2​δ​(c,c′)=1{\mathsf{Ham}}_{2\delta}(c,c^{\prime})=1

is negligible in n≥λn\geq\lambda. Since |C||C| is polynomial in λ\lambda, a union bound over all pairs implies that, with negligible probability, no pair of distinct codewords in CC are 𝖧𝖺𝗆2​δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{2\delta}-close. Consequently, if ζ\zeta is 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}-close to some codeword c∈Cc\in C, then it cannot be 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}-close to any other codeword in CC.

Combining this fact with 1, we have that whenever ζ\zeta is 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ−ϵ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta-\epsilon}-close to some block yy encoding a message mm, the ideal decoder outputs mm with all but negligible probability. Since the ideal decoder is indistinguishable from 𝖯𝖱𝖢.𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗏𝗄{\mathsf{PRC}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}_{\mathsf{vk}} to 𝒜\mathcal{A}, it follows that 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}} satisfies 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ−ϵ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta-\epsilon}-block robustness. ∎

The proof above relied on a simple fact, that random strings are far in Hamming distance with overwhelming probability.

Lemma 4.15.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} be any string length and let δ∈(0,12)\delta\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2}) be a fixed constant. Then

Prc,c′←{0,1}n[𝖧𝖺𝗆δ(c,c′)=1]≤negl(n).\Pr_{c,c^{\prime}\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{n}}\big[{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}(c,c^{\prime})=1\big]\leq\mathrm{negl}(n).
Proof.

For independently and uniformly random c,c′←{0,1}nc,c^{\prime}\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{n}, each coordinate differs with probability 1/21/2, so

𝔼⁡[‖c−c′‖0]=n2.\mathbb{E}\big[\|c-c^{\prime}\|_{0}\big]=\frac{n}{2}.

Applying a Chernoff bound with t=1−2​δ∈(0,1)t=1-2\delta\in(0,1), we get

Pr[∥c−c′∥0≤δn]≤exp(−n​(1−2​δ)24).\Pr\big[\|c-c^{\prime}\|_{0}\leq\delta n\big]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{n(1-2\delta)^{2}}{4}\right).

Since δ\delta is a constant strictly less than 1/21/2, the exponent is a negative constant times nn, and therefore the probability is negligible in nn. ∎

Public key block steganography in random oracle model.

Fairoze et al. [17] leverage random oracles to build a pubic key watermarking scheme. We observe that their scheme is implicitly built on top of a public key block steganography scheme, which we formalize in the following theorem.

Theorem 4.16 (Public key block steganography from random oracles [17]).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be any block size, and QQ be any language model satisfying the following entropy condition: for some ℓ=poly⁡(λ)\ell=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda), size ℓ\ell outputs from QQ have high min-entropy. That is,

∀π∈{0,1}∗,y←Q¯ℓ​(π)​ satisfies ​H∞​(y)≥ω⁡(log⁡λ).\forall\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*},y\leftarrow{\overline{Q}}_{\ell}(\pi)\text{ satisfies }H_{\infty}(y)\geq\omega(\log\lambda)\;.

For simplicity, assume ℓ\ell divides nn, so that n/ℓn/\ell is an integer.

Then there exists constants δ∈(0,12)\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{2}), ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) where in the random oracle model, there exists a block size nn public key Φδ\Phi_{\delta}-robust block steganography scheme with message size k=ρ⁡(n/ℓ−1)k=\rho(n/\ell-1), where Φδ:{0,1}n×{0,1}n→{0,1}\Phi_{\delta}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{n}\rightarrow\{0,1\} is the predicate

Φδ​(y,y′):(Parse (y1,…,yn/ℓ)=𝖡𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄𝗌(y),(y1′,…,yn/ℓ′)=𝖡𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄𝗌(y′) into ℓ-bit blocks,Output ​1​ iff ​y1=y1′​ and for a ​(1−δ)​-fraction of ​i∈{2,…,n/ℓ},yi=yi′).\Phi_{\delta}(y,y^{\prime}):\;\left(\begin{aligned} &\text{Parse }(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n/\ell})={\mathsf{Blocks}}(y),\;(y_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,y_{n/\ell}^{\prime})={\mathsf{Blocks}}(y^{\prime})\text{ into }\ell\text{-bit blocks},\\ &\text{Output }1\text{ iff }y_{1}=y_{1}^{\prime}\text{ and }\text{for a }(1-\delta)\text{-fraction of }i\in\{2,\ldots,n/\ell\},\;y_{i}=y_{i}^{\prime}\end{aligned}\right).
Proof.

We adapt the construction of [17]. Let (𝖤𝗇𝖼,𝖣𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Enc}},{\mathsf{Dec}}) be an information-theoretic error-correcting code with constant rate ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), that can correct up to a δ∈(0,12)\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{2}) fraction of errors1111 11 Such codes exists, for example [3, 34, 38].. Let H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} be independent random oracles. We define a block steganography scheme 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀=(𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼){\mathsf{Steg}}=({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}):

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ):{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}): samples r←{0,1}λr\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{\lambda} and outputs 𝗏𝗄=𝗌𝗄=r\mathsf{vk}=\mathsf{sk}=r.

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽⁡(r,π,m):{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Embed}}(r,\pi,m): first samples a block of ℓ\ell bits y1←Q¯ℓ​(π)y_{1}\leftarrow{\overline{Q}}_{\ell}(\pi), then computes the masked codeword

    c=(𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(m)⊕H2​((r,y1)))∈{0,1}n/ℓ−1.c=\Big({\mathsf{Enc}}(m)\oplus H_{2}\big((r,y_{1})\big)\Big)\in\{0,1\}^{n/\ell-1}\;.

    The algorithm then embeds cc into the next n/ℓ−1n/\ell-1 blocks of size ℓ\ell by rejection-sampling. That is,

    yi←Q¯ℓ​((,,,,,,,))​ conditioned on ​H1​((r,yi))=c⁡[i−1],y_{i}\leftarrow{\overline{Q}}_{\ell}\big((\pi,y_{1},\ldots,y_{i-1})\big)\text{ conditioned on }H_{1}\big((r,y_{i})\big)=c[i-1]\;,

    for i∈{2,…,n/ℓ}i\in\{2,\ldots,n/\ell\}. Then outputs y=(y1,…,yn/ℓ)∈{0,1}ny=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n/\ell})\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(r,ζ∈{0,1}n):{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{Ver}(r,\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{n}): parses ζ=(ζ1,…,ζn/ℓ)\zeta=(\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{n/\ell}) into blocks of size ℓ\ell, then computes

    𝗉𝖺𝖽=H2​((r,ζ1)), and ​c′​[i−1]=H1​((r,ζi))​ for ​i∈{2,…,n/ℓ},{\mathsf{pad}}=H_{2}\big((r,\zeta_{1})\big),\text{ and }c^{\prime}[i-1]=H_{1}\big((r,\zeta_{i})\big)\text{ for }i\in\{2,\ldots,n/\ell\},

    and outputs m=𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(c′⊕𝗉𝖺𝖽)m={\mathsf{Dec}}(c^{\prime}\oplus{\mathsf{pad}}).

Undetectability and the fact that the rejection sampling succeeds for every block with all but negligible probability follows directly from [17, Lemma 3.2]. Note that using their proof requires masking the message with the random oracle value of the first block H2​((r,y1))H_{2}\big((r,y_{1})\big).

To see robustness, let ζ=(ζ1,…,ζn/ℓ)←𝒜𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽r​(r)\zeta=(\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{n/\ell})\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Embed}}_{r}}(r), and suppose there exists (π,m,y)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽r)(\pi,m,y)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Embed}}_{r}}) with

Φδ​(ζ,y)=1.\Phi_{\delta}(\zeta,y)=1.

Denote (y1,…,yn/ℓ)(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n/\ell}) as the ℓ\ell-bit blocks of yy. By definition of Φδ\Phi_{\delta}, we have:

  1. 1.

    y1=ζ1y_{1}=\zeta_{1}, so the verifier 𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(r,ζ)\mathsf{Ver}(r,\zeta) recovers the pad, 𝗉𝖺𝖽=H2​((r,y1)){\mathsf{pad}}=H_{2}\big((r,y_{1})\big), exactly.

  2. 2.

    Among the blocks (ζ2,…,ζn/ℓ)(\zeta_{2},\ldots,\zeta_{n/\ell}), at most a δ\delta-fraction differ from the corresponding (y2,…,yn/ℓ)(y_{2},\ldots,y_{n/\ell}). Thus at most a δ\delta-fraction of the bits of c′c^{\prime} computed by 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖵𝖾𝗋{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{Ver} differ from the initial encoding c=𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(m)⊕𝗉𝖺𝖽c={\mathsf{Enc}}(m)\oplus{\mathsf{pad}}.

Because the error-correcting code can correct up to a δ\delta-fraction of errors, 𝖣𝖾𝖼⁡(c′⊕𝗉𝖺𝖽)=m{\mathsf{Dec}}(c^{\prime}\oplus{\mathsf{pad}})=m. ∎

5 Robust and Recoverable Digital Signatures

We present our formal definition of robust digital signatures, which allow verification even in the presence of small, adversarial perturbations to the message.

Definition 5.1 (Robust digital signatures with strong unforgeability).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter and let Φ\Phi be any predicate. A digital signature scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖵𝖾𝗋)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},\mathsf{Ver}) is robust and strongly unforgeable with respect to Φ\Phi if for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the scheme satisfies robustness,

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(ζ,σ)←𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄​(𝗉𝗄):(∃(y,σ)∈Π​ such that ​Φ​(ζ,y)=1)∧𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=0]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (\zeta,\sigma)&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{pk})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\;\Big(\exists(y,\sigma)\in\Pi\text{ such that }\Phi(\zeta,y)=1\Big)\\ \wedge\;\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)=0\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

and strong unforgeability,

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(ζ,σ)←𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄​(𝗉𝗄):𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=1∧(∀(y,σ)∈Π,Φ(ζ,y)=0)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (\zeta,\sigma)&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{pk})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\;\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)=1\\ \wedge\;\Big(\forall(y,\sigma)\in\Pi,\;\Phi(\zeta,y)=0\Big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi is the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

A recoverable digital signature scheme, in turn, requires a PPT recovery algorithm 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} that can recover the original message from its signature and a nearby, adversarially chosen input. For a digital signature scheme with message size n=n⁡(λ)n=n(\lambda), signature size k=k⁡(λ)k=k(\lambda), 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} has the syntax

  • •

    𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ):{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma): takes in the public key 𝗉𝗄\mathsf{pk}, a string ζ∈{0,1}n\zeta\in\{0,1\}^{n}, and a signature σ∈{0,1}k\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{k} and outputs a recovered message or a failure symbol y𝗋𝖾𝖼∈{0,1}n∪{⊥}y_{\mathsf{rec}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\cup\{\bot\}.

For 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} to satisfy strong unforgeability, any recovered message y𝗋𝖾𝖼y_{\mathsf{rec}} must indeed be close to the input ζ\zeta and must have been originally signed with the input signature σ\sigma.

Definition 5.2 (Recoverable digital signatures).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter and let Φ\Phi be any predicate. A digital signature scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) is recoverable with respect to Φ\Phi if for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the scheme is robustly recoverable, meaning

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(ζ,σ)←𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄​(𝗉𝗄)y𝗋𝖾𝖼←𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ):(∃(y,σ)∈Π​ such that ​Φ​(ζ,y)=1)∧y𝗋𝖾𝖼≠y]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (\zeta,\sigma)&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{pk})\\ y_{{\mathsf{rec}}}&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\;\Big(\exists(y,\sigma)\in\Pi\text{ such that }\Phi(\zeta,y)=1\Big)\\ \wedge\;y_{{\mathsf{rec}}}\neq y\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

and unforgeably recoverable, meaning

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(ζ,σ)←𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄​(𝗉𝗄)y𝗋𝖾𝖼←𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ):y𝗋𝖾𝖼≠⟂∧((y𝗋𝖾𝖼,σ)∉Π∨Φ⁡(ζ,y𝗋𝖾𝖼)=0)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (\zeta,\sigma)&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{pk})\\ y_{{\mathsf{rec}}}&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\;y_{{\mathsf{rec}}}\neq\perp\\ \;\wedge\;\Big((y_{{\mathsf{rec}}},\sigma)\notin\Pi\;\vee\;\Phi(\zeta,y_{{\mathsf{rec}}})=0\Big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi is the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

Another property we introduce is a notion of uniqueness for signatures. While this property is not required for our main result, it will be useful to guarantee a certain chaining property that we present in Section 6.2. A digital signature has unique signatures if no efficient adversary can produce an output ζ\zeta and two messages (y,y′)(y,y^{\prime}) with the same signature such that ζ\zeta is close to one message and far from another. Intuitively, this prevents an adversary from generating duplicate signatures on messages for which it can produce an intermediate output. Note that this property can be easily achieved by appending ω⁡(log⁡λ)\omega(\log\lambda) random bits to each signature, to ensure all signatures are almost surely unique. However, we show that our construction inherently satisfies it.

Definition 5.3 (Unique signatures).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter and let Φ\Phi be any predicate. A digital signature scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖵𝖾𝗋)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},\mathsf{Ver}) has unique signatures with respect to Φ\Phi, if for any PPT 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(ζ,y,y′)←𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄​(𝗉𝗄):(Φ⁡(ζ,y)=1∧Φ⁡(ζ,y′)=0)∧(∃σ​ such that ​(y,σ)∈Π​ and ​(y′,σ)∈Π)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (\zeta,y,y^{\prime})\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{pk})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\;\Big(\Phi(\zeta,y)=1\;\wedge\;\Phi(\zeta,y^{\prime})=0\Big)\\ \wedge\;\Big(\exists\sigma\text{ such that }(y,\sigma)\in\Pi\text{ and }(y^{\prime},\sigma)\in\Pi\Big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi is the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}).

5.1 Difference-recovering hash family

The core ingredient of our signature scheme is a property-preserving hashing scheme (PPH) [11]. We observe that existing Hamming PPH constructions [19, 26] support recovery of the bitwise difference Δ=x⊕x′\Delta=x\oplus x^{\prime} between two close strings xx and x′x^{\prime} using only their hashes h⁡(x)h(x) and h⁡(x′)h(x^{\prime}). We define a slightly weaker property than this, which requires recovering the difference between two inputs when one of the inputs is given in the clear. This property is sufficient for watermarking applications, and we show that it can be achieved by any PPH for the Hamming predicate. In Section A, we define the stronger variant, which requires recovering the difference using only the hashes of both inputs.

Definition 5.4 (Difference recovering PPH).

For any predicate Φ\Phi, a hash family (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,{ℋλ})({\mathsf{Sample}},\{\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}\}) is difference-recovering w.r.t. Φ\Phi if there exists a PPT algorithm 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} such that for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr⁡[h←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)(x,x′)←𝒜⁡(1λ,h)Δ←𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(h,h⁡(x),x′):(Δ≠x⊕x′∧Φ⁡(x,x′)=1)∨(Δ≠⊥∧Φ(x,x′)=0)]≤negl⁡(λ)\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}h&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (x,x^{\prime})&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(1^{\lambda},h)\\ \Delta&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Rec}}(h,h(x),x^{\prime})\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\big(\Delta\neq x\oplus x^{\prime}\wedge\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=1\big)\\ \vee\;\big(\Delta\neq\bot\wedge\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=0\big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)
Proposition 5.5.

Let λ\lambda be the security parameter. For any input size n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) and threshold r=poly⁡(λ)r=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) such that r<n/2r<n/2, every 𝖧𝖺𝗆r/n{\mathsf{Ham}}_{r/n}-PPH supports difference recovery w.r.t. 𝖧𝖺𝗆r/n{\mathsf{Ham}}_{r/n}.

Proof.

Let h←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)h\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda}). We construct a recovery algorithm 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(h,⋅,⋅){\mathsf{Rec}}(h,\cdot,\cdot) which, given a hash h⁡(x)h(x) and an input x′x^{\prime} in the clear, returns the difference x⊕x′x\oplus x^{\prime} if 𝖧𝖺𝗆r/n​(x,x′)=1{\mathsf{Ham}}_{r/n}(x,x^{\prime})=1, and returns ⊥\bot otherwise. The recovery algorithm only needs oracle access to 𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(h,⋅){\mathsf{Hash}}(h,\cdot) and 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅(h,h(x),⋅){\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),\cdot). For the reader’s convenience, we include the pseudocode for 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} in Figure 3.

We may assume that 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(x),h⁡(ζ))=𝖧𝖺𝗆r/n​(x,ζ){\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),h(\zeta))={\mathsf{Ham}}_{r/n}(x,\zeta) for all inputs ζ∈𝔽2n\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} used by 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} to query 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅(h,h(x),⋅){\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),\cdot), since 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} is an efficient deterministic algorithm. Any violation would contradict the direct-access robustness of the underlying Hamming PPH.

If 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(x),h⁡(x′))=0{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),h(x^{\prime}))=0, then 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(h,h⁡(x),x′){\mathsf{Rec}}(h,h(x),x^{\prime}) returns ⊥\bot, which is fine since 𝖧𝖺𝗆r/n​(x,x′)=𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(x),h⁡(x′))=0{\mathsf{Ham}}_{r/n}(x,x^{\prime})={\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),h(x^{\prime}))=0.

If 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(x),h⁡(x′))=1{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),h(x^{\prime}))=1, then 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(h,h⁡(x),x′){\mathsf{Rec}}(h,h(x),x^{\prime}) needs to return the difference x⊕x′x\oplus x^{\prime}. To this end, it first finds a boundary point relative to xx. That is, a point ζ∈𝔽2n\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} such that ‖x⊕ζ‖0=r\|x\oplus\zeta\|_{0}=r. Once such a point is found, difference recovery is straightforward: since we know that ζ⊕x\zeta\oplus x is rr-sparse, we can determine its support of the by flipping each bit of ζ\zeta individually. Specifically, for each j∈[n]j\in[n], we test whether 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(x),h⁡(ζ⊕ej))=1{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),h(\zeta\oplus e_{j}))=1, where ej∈𝔽2ne_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} denotes the jj-th standard basis vector (i.e., the vector with a 11 in the jj-th position and zeros elsewhere). We conclude that jj lies in the support of x⊕ζx\oplus\zeta if and only if the evaluation remains 11 after the one-bit perturbation.

We now describe an efficient procedure for finding a boundary point ζ\zeta with respect to xx, given h⁡(x)h(x) and x′x^{\prime} satisfying ‖x⊕x′‖0≤r\|x\oplus x^{\prime}\|_{0}\leq r. For any j∈[n]j\in[n], define

uj\displaystyle u_{j} =e1⊕⋯⊕ej,ζj=x′⊕uj.\displaystyle=e_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus e_{j}\;,\quad\zeta_{j}=x^{\prime}\oplus u_{j}\;.

Define the potential function f:{0,1,…,n}→{0,1,…,n}f:\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\} by

f⁡(j)=‖x⊕ζj‖0,\displaystyle f(j)=\|x\oplus\zeta_{j}\|_{0}\;,

with f⁡(0)=‖x⊕x′‖0f(0)=\|x\oplus x^{\prime}\|_{0}.

Observe that for each j<nj<n, we have |f⁡(j+1)−f⁡(j)|=1|f(j+1)-f(j)|=1. In other words, the value of f⁡(j)f(j) always changes by either 11 or −1-1. In addition, it holds that f⁡(0)≤rf(0)\leq r and f⁡(n)=n−f⁡(0)>rf(n)=n-f(0)>r. Thus, by the discrete intermediate value property, there exists s∈{0,1,…,n}s\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\} such that f⁡(s)=rf(s)=r. The corresponding ζs\zeta_{s} is the desired boundary point.

Although 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} cannot explicitly compute f⁡(j)f(j), it can determine whether f⁡(j)≤rf(j)\leq r by querying 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(x),h⁡(ζj)){\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),h(\zeta_{j})). The algorithm increments jj from 11 to nn, stopping at the first index where 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{Eval}} returns 00. Let jj be the smallest such index. Then the boundary point is ζj−1\zeta_{j-1}. ∎

Difference recovery from standard CRHF.

Proposition 5.5 implies that the PPH from homomorphic CRHFs given in Theorem 4.7 satisfies difference recovery with respect to 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}. However, the converse does not hold. In particular, one can instantiate a difference recovering hash family for Hamming that does not admit an evaluation algorithm 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{Eval}} for computing the predicate on two hashes, as the recovery algorithm 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} receives one of its inputs in the clear. This instantiation is heavily inspired by the notion and construction of secure sketches [16]. We refer the reader to Section B for additional details.

Theorem 5.6 (Sharp sketch for Hamming, adapted from [16, Section 8.3]).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) denote the input size. Suppose there exists a CRHF with output size ℓ=ℓ⁡(λ)\ell=\ell(\lambda). For any constants δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and ρ>H2𝖡𝖹​(δ)\rho>H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta), where H2𝖡𝖹​(⋅)H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\cdot) refers to the Blokh-Zyablov bound, there exists a difference recovering hash family (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) w.r.t. 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta} that has hash size ρ⋅n+ℓ\rho\cdot n+\ell.

Remark 5.7 (Comparison with Theorem 4.7).

The hash family from Theorem 5.6 requires only a standard collision-resistant hash function, not a homomorphic one. Moreover, it uses efficiently list-decodable codes over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}, whereas Theorem 4.7 uses codes over 𝔽3\mathbb{F}_{3}. As a result, it benefits from the Blokh-Zyablov bound over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} and avoids the multiplicative factor of log2⁡3\log_{2}3 in the hash size. However, it is not a PPH.

5.2 Robust signature from PPH

We now prove a generic theorem showing that the construction presented in Section 2.1 is both robust and unforgeable with respect to Φ\Phi. In Section 5.4, we instantiate the theorem with an existing Hamming PPH [26]. We recall the construction in Figure 4.

Theorem 5.8 (Generic robust signatures).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be any message size, and Φ\Phi be any predicate. If 𝖯𝖯𝖧⁡[𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁,𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅]{\mathsf{PPH}}[{\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Hash}},{\mathsf{Eval}}] is a Φ\Phi-PPH with hash size k=poly⁡(λ)k=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) and 𝖣𝖲𝖲⁡[𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖵𝖾𝗋]{\mathsf{DSS}}[{\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},\mathsf{Ver}] is a strongly unforgeable digital signature scheme with signature size ℓ=poly⁡(λ)\ell=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda), then (𝖱𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖱𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋)({\mathsf{RGen}},{\mathsf{RSign}},{\mathsf{RVer}}), defined in Figure 4, is a robust and unforgeable signature scheme for Φ\Phi with signature size k+ℓk+\ell. Moreover, the scheme has unique signatures with respect to Φ\Phi.

Proof.

Robustness of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}} follows immediately from the correctness of the underlying 𝖣𝖲𝖲{\mathsf{DSS}} and the direct-access robustness of 𝖯𝖯𝖧{\mathsf{PPH}}. We focus on proving strong unforgeability. Assume for contradiction that there exists a PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} that outputs a pair (ζ,σ)(\zeta,\sigma) such that Φ⁡(ζ,y)=0\Phi(\zeta,y)=0 for all (y,σ)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖱𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇)(y,\sigma)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RSign}}}) but the pair passes 𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋{\mathsf{RVer}} with non-negligible probability.

That is, let (𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄)←𝖱𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ)({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{RGen}}(1^{\lambda}), (ζ,σ)←𝒜𝖱𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄)(\zeta,\sigma)\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RSign}}_{{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk}}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk}), and let Π\Pi denote the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖱𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RSign}}}), where each entry logs a tuple (y,z,τ)(y,z,\tau), with z=h⁡(y)z=h(y) and τ=𝖣𝖲𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇(𝖣𝖲𝖲.𝗉𝗄,z)\tau={\mathsf{DSS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}({\mathsf{DSS}}.\mathsf{pk},z). Then there exists a polynomial q:ℕ→ℕq:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} such that

Pr⁡[𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=1∧∀(y,z,τ)∈Π,Φ(ζ,y)=0]>1/q⁡(λ).\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}{\mathsf{RVer}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)=1\\ \wedge\;\forall(y,z,\tau)\in\Pi,\Phi(\zeta,y)=0\end{array}\right]>1/q(\lambda)\;.

Let E𝖣𝖲𝖲E_{{\mathsf{DSS}}} denote the event that σ=(z,τ)\sigma=(z,\tau) constitutes a successful forgery against 𝖣𝖲𝖲{\mathsf{DSS}} , and let E𝖯𝖯𝖧E_{{\mathsf{PPH}}} denote the event that (ζ,z)(\zeta,z) violates the direct-access robustness of 𝖯𝖯𝖧{\mathsf{PPH}}. More precisely,

E𝖣𝖲𝖲\displaystyle E_{\mathsf{DSS}} =𝖣𝖲𝖲.𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗉𝗄,z,τ)=1∧(⋅,z,τ)∉Π,\displaystyle={\mathsf{DSS}}.\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{pk},z,\tau)=1\;\wedge\;(\cdot,z,\tau)\not\in\Pi\;,
E𝖯𝖯𝖧\displaystyle E_{\mathsf{PPH}} =𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(ζ),z)=1∧⋁(y,z,τ)∈ΠΦ⁡(ζ,y)=0,\displaystyle={\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(\zeta),z)=1\;\wedge\;\bigvee_{(y,z,\tau)\in\Pi}\Phi(\zeta,y)=0\;,

where (⋅,z,τ)∉Π(\cdot,z,\tau)\not\in\Pi is shorthand for ∄y​ such that ​(y,z,τ)∈Π\not\exists y\text{ such that }(y,z,\tau)\in\Pi. Since

𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=𝖣𝖲𝖲.𝖵𝖾𝗋(𝖣𝖲𝖲.𝗉𝗄,z,τ)∧𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅(h,h(ζ),z),{\mathsf{RVer}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)={\mathsf{DSS}}.\mathsf{Ver}({\mathsf{DSS}}.\mathsf{pk},z,\tau)\wedge{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(\zeta),z)\;,

we observe that

𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=1∧(∀(y,σ)\displaystyle{\mathsf{RVer}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)=1\;\wedge\;(\forall(y,\sigma) ∈Π,Φ(ζ,y)=0)⊆E𝖣𝖲𝖲∨(E𝖯𝖯𝖧∧(⋅,z,τ)∈Π).\displaystyle\in\Pi,\Phi(\zeta,y)=0)\subseteq E_{\mathsf{DSS}}\vee(E_{\mathsf{PPH}}\wedge(\cdot,z,\tau)\in\Pi)\;.

It follows that Pr⁡[E𝖣𝖲𝖲∨(E𝖯𝖯𝖧∧(⋅,z,τ)∈Π)]>1/q⁡(λ)\Pr\left[E_{\mathsf{DSS}}\vee(E_{\mathsf{PPH}}\wedge(\cdot,z,\tau)\in\Pi)\right]>1/q(\lambda). This leads to a contradiction, since both E𝖣𝖲𝖲E_{{\mathsf{DSS}}} and E𝖯𝖯𝖧∧(⋅,z,τ)∈ΠE_{{\mathsf{PPH}}}\wedge(\cdot,z,\tau)\in\Pi should occur with negligible probability due to the the strong unforgeability of 𝖣𝖲𝖲{\mathsf{DSS}}, and the direct-access robustness of 𝖯𝖯𝖧{\mathsf{PPH}} respectively. Therefore, the robust signature scheme for Φ\Phi presented in Figure 4 is strongly unforgeable.

Unique signatures.

Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there exists an adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} and a polynomial q:ℕ→ℕq:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} such that for (𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖱𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{RGen}}(1^{\lambda}) and (ζ,y,y′)←𝒜𝖱𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄​(𝗉𝗄)(\zeta,y,y^{\prime})\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RSign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{pk}) ,

Pr⁡[∃σ​ such that ​(y,σ)∈Π​ and ​(y′,σ)∈Π∧Φ⁡(ζ,y)=1∧Φ⁡(ζ,y′)=0]>1/q⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}\;\exists\sigma\text{ such that }(y,\sigma)\in\Pi\text{ and }(y^{\prime},\sigma)\in\Pi\\ \wedge\;\Phi(\zeta,y)=1\;\wedge\;\Phi(\zeta,y^{\prime})=0\end{array}\right]>1/q(\lambda)\;,

Then 𝒜\mathcal{A} finds yy and y′y^{\prime} such that h⁡(y)=h⁡(y′)h(y)=h(y^{\prime}), where hh is the PPH hash function, with probability at least 1/q⁡(λ)1/q(\lambda), because their signatures are identical. However, this implies that either the pair (ζ,y)(\zeta,y) or (ζ,y′)(\zeta,y^{\prime}) violates the robustness of 𝖯𝖯𝖧{\mathsf{PPH}}. Specifically, the evaluation algorithm 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{Eval}} cannot distinguish h⁡(y)h(y) from h⁡(y′)h(y^{\prime}), and hence 𝖯𝖯𝖧.𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(y),h⁡(ζ))​ and ​𝖯𝖯𝖧.𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(y′),h⁡(ζ)){\mathsf{PPH}}.{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(y),h(\zeta))\text{ and }{\mathsf{PPH}}.{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(y^{\prime}),h(\zeta)) will have the same output distribution, even though Φ⁡(ζ,y)≠Φ⁡(ζ,y′)\Phi(\zeta,y)\neq\Phi(\zeta,y^{\prime}). Therefore, at least one of these pairs must cause 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{Eval}} to output the incorrect predicate value with inverse-polynomial probability, contradicting the robustness of 𝖯𝖯𝖧{\mathsf{PPH}}. ∎

5.3 Recoverable signatures from difference-recovering PPH

We show that our generic construction from Theorem 5.8 is recoverable, provided the underlying 𝖯𝖯𝖧{\mathsf{PPH}} is difference recovering. Let (𝖱𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖱𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{RGen}},{\mathsf{RSign}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) denote the scheme from Figure 4, where the verification algorithm 𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋{\mathsf{RVer}} is replaced by the recovery algorithm 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} presented in Algorithm 8. The guarantees of this scheme are formally stated in Corollary 5.9.

Corollary 5.9 (Recoverable signatures).

Let Φ\Phi be any predicate. If 𝖯𝖯𝖧⁡[𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁,𝖱𝖾𝖼]{\mathsf{PPH}}[{\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Hash}},{\mathsf{Rec}}] is difference recovering w.r.t. Φ\Phi (as in Definition 5.4) and 𝖣𝖲𝖲⁡[𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖵𝖾𝗋]{\mathsf{DSS}}[{\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},\mathsf{Ver}] is a strongly unforgeable digital signature scheme, then the resulting (𝖱𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖱𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{RGen}},{\mathsf{RSign}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) is a recoverable digital signature scheme w.r.t. Φ\Phi.

Remark 5.10 (Recoverable signatures without PPH).

Note that Corollary 5.9 can be instantiated using any difference recovering hash family, not necessarily a PPH. Although 𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋{\mathsf{RVer}}, invoked by 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}}, leverages PPH evaluation 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(ζ),z){\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(\zeta),z), this call can instead be replaced by computing Φ(ζ,𝖯𝖯𝖧.𝖱𝖾𝖼(h,z,ζ)⊕ζ)\Phi(\zeta,{\mathsf{PPH}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}(h,z,\zeta)\oplus\zeta). We present the construction using 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{Eval}} only because PPHs are widely studied.

Proof.

Let (𝗉𝗄=(h,𝖣𝖲𝖲.𝗉𝗄),𝗌𝗄)←𝖱𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ)(\mathsf{pk}=(h,{\mathsf{DSS}}.\mathsf{pk}),\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{RGen}}(1^{\lambda}) and let ζ←𝒜𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄​(𝗉𝗄)\zeta\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{pk}) be the adversary’s output.

Robust recovery.

Suppose there exists yy such that (y,σ)∈Π(y,\sigma)\in\Pi and Φ⁡(ζ,y)=1\Phi(\zeta,y)=1. By robustness of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}, 𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=1{\mathsf{RVer}}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)=1 with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda). Conditioned on this, σ=(h⁡(y),⋅)\sigma=(h(y),\cdot), and the difference-recovery of 𝖯𝖯𝖧{\mathsf{PPH}} satisfies 𝖯𝖯𝖧.𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(h,h⁡(y),ζ)=y⊕ζ{\mathsf{PPH}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}(h,h(y),\zeta)=y\oplus\zeta with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda), so the final output is yy with overwhelming probability.

Unforgeable recovery.

Suppose 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=y𝗋𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)=y_{{\mathsf{rec}}}, with y𝗋𝖾𝖼≠⟂y_{{\mathsf{rec}}}\neq\perp. Then by definition of 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}}, 𝖱𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗉𝗄,ζ,σ)=1{\mathsf{RVer}}(\mathsf{pk},\zeta,\sigma)=1. By strong unforgeability of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}, with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda) there exists yy such that (y,σ)∈Π(y,\sigma)\in\Pi and Φ⁡(ζ,y)=1\Phi(\zeta,y)=1, meaning σ=(h⁡(y),⋅)\sigma=(h(y),\cdot) corresponds to a valid signature of yy.

Conditioned on the above, difference-recovery of 𝖯𝖯𝖧{\mathsf{PPH}} yields 𝖯𝖯𝖧.𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(h,h⁡(y)CLOSE,{\mathsf{PPH}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}(h,h(y), OPENζ)\zeta) =y⊕ζ=y\oplus\zeta with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda), meaning

y𝗋𝖾𝖼=ζ⊕𝖯𝖯𝖧.𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(h,h⁡(y),ζ)=ζ⊕(y⊕ζ)=y,y_{{\mathsf{rec}}}=\zeta\oplus{\mathsf{PPH}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}(h,h(y),\zeta)=\zeta\oplus(y\oplus\zeta)=y,

which implies that y𝗋𝖾𝖼y_{{\mathsf{rec}}} satisfies (y𝗋𝖾𝖼,σ)∈Π(y_{{\mathsf{rec}}},\sigma)\in\Pi and Φ⁡(ζ,y𝗋𝖾𝖼)=1\Phi(\zeta,y_{{\mathsf{rec}}})=1. Since the intersection of both events occurs with overwhelming probability, the claim follows. ∎

5.4 Instantiating Hamming signatures

We instantiate a recoverable digital signature scheme for Hamming predicates, providing concrete trade-offs between the signature size kk (relative to the message length nn) and the tolerable Hamming error rr. Since the regime of practical interest in watermarking corresponds to a constant error rate r/n=Ω⁡(1)r/n=\Omega(1), we focus on the rates achievable in this setting.

Here, we refer to the signature-to-message rate, k/nk/n of a RDS with signature size kk, message size nn.

Corollary 5.11 (Recoverable digital signatures with constant error-rate).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and suppose there exists a CRHF with output size ℓ=ℓ⁡(λ)\ell=\ell(\lambda) and a strongly unforgeable digital signature scheme with signature size k=k⁡(λ)k=k(\lambda). Let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) such that (ℓ+k)/n=o⁡(1)(\ell+k)/n=o(1) be the message size. For any constants δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and ρ>H2𝖡𝖹​(δ)\rho>H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta), where H2𝖡𝖹​(⋅)H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\cdot) denotes the Blokh–Zyablov bound, there exists a recoverable digital signature scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) for the predicate 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta} over {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} with signature-to-message rate ρ+o⁡(1)\rho+o(1). Moreover, the scheme has unique signatures with respect to 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}.

Proof.

We instantiate Corollary 5.9 using the difference recovering hash family from Theorem 5.6 for the predicate 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}. The hash size is ρ​n+ℓ\rho n+\ell, and signing the hash incurs an additional kk bits. Thus, the total signature size is ρ​n+ℓ+k\rho n+\ell+k, and the resulting recoverable signature-to-message rate is (ρ​n+ℓ+k)/n=ρ+o⁡(1)(\rho n+\ell+k)/n=\rho+o(1). ∎

Remark 5.12.

We instantiate our construction using a sharp sketch (Theorem 5.6) rather than a PPH. Note that we could alternatively use the PPH from Theorem 4.7, with recoverability following from Proposition 5.5. However, using a secure sketch offers the advantage that we can achieve any constant ρ>H2𝖡𝖹​(δ)\rho>H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta) (rather than ρ>H3𝖡𝖹​(δ)​log2​3\rho>H_{3}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta)\log_{2}3), and that we can rely only on CRHFs instead of homomorphic CRHFs.

We can also instantiate signatures that achieve a subconstant error rate, by using a sharp sketch and analysis along the lines of [26, Corollary 6.8].

Corollary 5.13 (Recoverable digital signatures with subconstant error-rate).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and suppose there exists a CRHF with output size ℓ=ℓ⁡(λ)\ell=\ell(\lambda) and a strongly unforgeable digital signature scheme with signature size k=k⁡(λ)k=k(\lambda). Let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be the message size. For any δ=o⁡(1)\delta=o(1), there exists a recoverable digital signature scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) for the predicate 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta} with signature size O⁡(δ​n​log⁡n)+ℓ+kO(\delta n\log n)+\ell+k. Moreover, the scheme has unique signatures with respect to 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}.

6 Recoverable, Robust, and Unforgeable Watermarking

In Section 6.1, we present our main construction, which combines block steganography with robust signatures to obtain a robust and unforgeable watermarking scheme. We then demonstrate, in Section 6.2, that our verification algorithm can be generalized by chaining across longer substrings, yielding fine-grained control over the tradeoff in substring size between robustness and unforgeability. In Section 6.3, we prove that if the underlying signature scheme is recoverable, we can build a recoverable watermarking scheme. Finally, in Section 6.4, we instantiate both secret and public key versions of our construction using existing block steganography constructions [14, 4, 17] together with our robust and recoverable digital signature instantiations (Corollaries 5.11 and 5.13).

6.1 Robust and unforgeable watermarking

Theorem 6.1 summarizes the guarantees of our watermarking scheme. It has the following properties

  • •

    (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],2​n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],2n)-robustness: an (adversarially chosen) ζ\zeta verifies if it contains a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta of size 2​n2n whose two blocks (ζ1∗,ζ2∗)(\zeta_{1}^{*},\zeta_{2}^{*}) are Φ\Phi-close to two consecutive response blocks (yt,yt+1)(y_{t},y_{t+1}).

  • •

    (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],n)-unforgeability: whenever ζ\zeta verifies, there exists an nn-sized substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta that is Φ\Phi-close to some response block yty_{t}.

The parameters Φ\Phi and nn are inherited from the underlying block steganography and robust signature schemes. Whether robustness is secret key or public key depends on the block steganography scheme. In contrast, unforgeability is inherited entirely from the robust signature and is therefore always public key. Compared to the basic watermarking scheme obtained directly from block steganography (Fact 4.13), our construction yields slightly weaker robustness—requiring a 2​n2n-sized close substring to verify rather than an nn-sized substring—but additionally provides unforgeability (and, as we show in Section 6.3, recoverability).

Theorem 6.1 (Robust and unforgeable 2-block watermarking).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and let k,n=poly⁡(λ)k,n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be any message and block size, respectively. Let Φ\Phi be any closeness predicate, and QQ be any language model. Suppose that:

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀⁡[𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼]{\mathsf{Steg}}[{\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}] is a message size kk, block size nn block steganography scheme for QQ with (secret or public key) Φ\Phi-robustness (Definition 4.11).

  • •

    𝖱𝖣𝖲⁡[𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖵𝖾𝗋]{\mathsf{RDS}}[{\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},\mathsf{Ver}] is a message size nn, signature size kk Φ\Phi-robust digital signature scheme (Definition 5.1).

Then the construction (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖵𝖾𝗋)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},\mathsf{Ver}) in Figure 5 is a watermarking scheme for QQ with (secret or public key) (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],2​n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],2n)-robustness, and public key (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],n)-unforgeability, where 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n] is defined as in Definition 3.2.

We present the full details of our watermarking scheme (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖵𝖾𝗋)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},\mathsf{Ver}), then prove the theorem. The construction is the same whether 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}} is public or secret key, but its guarantees change. The 𝖦𝖾𝗇{\mathsf{Gen}} algorithm generates the watermarking and verification keys.

Given a prompt x∈{0,1}∗x\in\{0,1\}^{*}, the watermarking algorithm 𝖶𝖺𝗍{\mathsf{Wat}} generates a response by sampling text blocks of size n=n⁡(λ)n=n(\lambda) sequentially and embedding the robust signature associated with each block into the next.

The verification algorithm 𝖵𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Ver} operates on arbitrary sized strings, by using 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}} to recover embedded signatures and checking whether any 2​n2n-sized substring in the input corresponds to a valid message-signature pair.

Proof.

Undetectability follows directly from the undetectability of 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}}. For robustness and unforgeability, fix λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} and a PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Let

(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄)←𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ),(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄)←𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ).({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}),\quad({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\;.

Denote 𝗏𝗄=(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,\mathsf{vk}=({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk}, 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄){\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk}) and 𝗌𝗄=(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄)\mathsf{sk}=({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk},{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk}). Let ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄​(𝗏𝗄)\zeta\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{vk}).

Robustness.

We prove the public key version; the secret-key version follows by an analogous argument. Suppose there exists a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta with |ζ∗|=2​n|\zeta^{*}|=2n and a prompt-response pair (x,y)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄)(x,y)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}) such that ζ∗\zeta^{*} is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-close to yy. We will show 𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=1\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=1 with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda). Denote (ζ1∗,ζ2∗)=𝖡𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄𝗌⁡(ζ∗)(\zeta^{*}_{1},\zeta^{*}_{2})={\mathsf{Blocks}}(\zeta^{*}). The closeness condition says that there exists a block index t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} such that

Φ⁡(ζ1∗,yt)=1​ and ​Φ​(ζ2∗,yt+1)=1.\Phi(\zeta^{*}_{1},y_{t})=1\text{ and }\Phi(\zeta^{*}_{2},y_{t+1})=1\;.

Moreover, because yt+1y_{t+1} is an nn-sized block returned by 𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}, and it isn’t the first block y1y_{1}, it has the signature of the previous block yty_{t} embedded in it. That is,

((π=(x,y1,…,yt),m=σt),yt+1)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄)\Big(\big(\pi=(x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{t}),m=\sigma_{t}\big),y_{t+1}\Big)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Embed}}_{{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk}}})

where σt\sigma_{t} is the 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}} signature of yty_{t} computed during an oracle call to 𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄​(x){\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}(x).

The closeness of the second half Φ⁡(ζ2∗,yt+1)=1\Phi(\zeta^{*}_{2},y_{t+1})=1, together with the block robustness of 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}}, ensures that 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖣𝖾𝖼(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,ζ2∗)=σt{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*}_{2})=\sigma_{t} with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda). Conditioned on this event, the closeness of the first half Φ⁡(ζ1∗,yt)=1\Phi(\zeta^{*}_{1},y_{t})=1, together with the robustness of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}, ensures that 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ1∗,σt)=1{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*}_{1},\sigma_{t})=1 with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda).

If both events occur, then 𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=1\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=1, since it accepts if any 2​n2n-substring of ζ\zeta verifies under this two-part check. Because both events occur with all but negligible probability, successful verification also occurs with all but negligible probability.

Unforgeability.

Let Π\Pi denote the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}). Suppose, towards contradiction, that there exists a polynomial q:ℕ→ℕq:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N} such that

Pr⁡[𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=1∧¬(∃ζ∗⪯ζ,(x,y)∈Π such that OPEN𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]​(ζ∗,y)=1∧|ζ∗|=n)]≥1/q⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=1\\ \wedge\;\neg\big(\exists\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta,(x,y)\in\Pi\text{ such that }\\ \mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n](\zeta^{*},y)=1\;\wedge\;|\zeta^{*}|=n\big)\end{array}\right]\geq 1/q(\lambda)\;,
