Note that the set of all such blocks yty_{t} subsumes the set of message for which 𝒜\mathcal{A} observed robust signatures, because the only messages that 𝒜\mathcal{A} sees signatures for during interaction with 𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}} are response blocks yty_{t}. This means that for all ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta such that |ζ∗|=n|\zeta^{*}|=n, and for all (y,⋅)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄),Φ⁡(ζ∗,y)=0.(y,\cdot)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}_{{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk}}}),\;\Phi(\zeta^{*},y)=0.

However, under the same event, 𝖵𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=1\mathsf{Ver}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=1, meaning 𝒜\mathcal{A} found some ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta of size nn and some σ∈{0,1}k\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{k} such that 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖵𝖾𝗋(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ∗,σ)=1{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{Ver}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta^{*},\sigma)=1 with probability at least 1/q⁡(λ)1/q(\lambda). These two facts combined contradict the unforgeability of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}.

∎

6.2 Generalizing verification to chains

The verification algorithm for our watermarking scheme (Figure 5) applies a sliding window to ζ\zeta, checking whether any substring of size 2​n2n contains a valid message–signature pair. As a result, Theorem 6.1 guarantees unforgeability with respect to substrings of size nn (the size of the signed message).

We can generalize this approach by using a sliding window of size r​nrn for any r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} with r≥2r\geq 2. Within each r​nrn-bit window, we can verify that the entire chain of rr, nn-bit blocks verifies back-to-back. This yields a stronger unforgeability guarantee: successful verification implies the existence of an (r−1)​n(r-1)n-bit substring in ζ\zeta that is close to a consecutive chain of blocks, (yt,…,yt+r−2)(y_{t},\ldots,y_{t+r-2}), present in a single observed response. We formally define a family of general verification algorithms, {𝖵𝖾𝗋r}r∈ℕ\{\mathsf{Ver}_{r}\}_{r\in\mathbb{N}}, in Figure 6.

Chain verification takes rr blocks of size nn as input and verifies that for each consecutive pair of blocks (ζj∗,ζj+1∗)(\zeta_{j}^{*},\zeta_{j+1}^{*}), the signature recovered from the second block successfully verifies with the message given by the first. If any block fails verification, the entire chain is rejected.

Theorem 6.2 states the guarantees obtained when instead using 𝖵𝖾𝗋r\mathsf{Ver}_{r} as the verifier for our construction. Its guarantees differ from those obtained using 2-block verification in two respects. First, chain verification requires that 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}} has unique signatures ( Definition 5.3), though, as noted previously, this is not particularly restrictive. Second, unlike in the 2-block case, whether unforgeability holds in the public or secret key setting additionally depends on the robustness guarantees of the underlying block steganography scheme 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}}.

Theorem 6.2 (Robust and unforgeable rr-block watermarking).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, let r=poly⁡(λ)r=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) satisfying r≥2r\geq 2 be any chain size, and let k,n=poly⁡(λ)k,n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be any message and block size, respectively. Let Φ\Phi be any closeness predicate, and QQ be any language model. Suppose that:

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀⁡[𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼]{\mathsf{Steg}}[{\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}] is a message size kk, block size nn block steganography scheme for QQ with (secret or public key) Φ\Phi-robustness (Definition 4.11).

  • •

    𝖱𝖣𝖲⁡[𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖵𝖾𝗋]{\mathsf{RDS}}[{\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},\mathsf{Ver}] is a message size nn, signature size kk Φ\Phi-robust digital signature scheme (Definition 5.1) that has unique signatures w.r.t. Φ\Phi (Definition 5.3).

Then the construction (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖵𝖾𝗋r)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},\mathsf{Ver}_{r}) (Figures 5 and 6) is a watermarking scheme for QQ with (secret or public key) (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],r​n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],rn)-robustness, and (secret or public key) (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],(r−1)​n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],(r-1)n)-unforgeability.

Proof.

Undetectability and robustness are straightforward from the robustness and undetectability of 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}} and the robustness of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}. Therefore, we will focus on proving the unforgeability guarantee. We will prove secret key unforgeability; public key follows analogously.

Fix λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} and a PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Let

(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄)←𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ),(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄)←𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ).({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}),\quad({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\;.

Denote 𝗏𝗄=(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄)\mathsf{vk}=({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk}) and 𝗌𝗄=(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄)\mathsf{sk}=({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk},{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk}). Let Π\Pi denote the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}) and let ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄,(𝖵𝖾𝗋r)𝗏𝗄​(1λ)\zeta\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}},(\mathsf{Ver}_{r})_{\mathsf{vk}}}(1^{\lambda})

We begin by showing that the event that a string ζ\zeta is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-far from every response yy implies a more convenient event. For a predicate Φ\Phi and an index i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, define

𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ζ,Π):=(∃ℓ∈ℕ​ such that ​|ζ|=ℓ​n​ and (i>ℓ​ or ​∃(x,y)∈Π​ such that CLOSEOPENOPEN𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]​((ζi,…,ζℓ),y)=1))).\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,i}(\zeta,\Pi):=\left(\begin{aligned} &\exists\ell\in\mathbb{N}\text{ such that }|\zeta|=\ell n\text{ and }\\ &\Big(i>\ell\text{ or }\exists(x,y)\in\Pi\text{ such that }\\ &\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]\big((\zeta_{i},\ldots,\zeta_{\ell}),\,y\big)=1\big)\Big)\end{aligned}\right). (2)

Given a sequence ζ=(ζ1,…,ζℓ)\zeta=(\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{\ell}) of ℓ\ell blocks of size nn, the event asserts that the suffix starting at the iith block, (ζi,…,ζℓ)(\zeta_{i},\ldots,\zeta_{\ell}) is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-close to some response yy appearing in the transcript Π\Pi. When i>ℓi>\ell, we interpret 𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ζCLOSE,\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,i}(\zeta, OPENΠ)=1\Pi)=1.

Now notice that if a string ζ=(ζ1,…,ζℓ)\zeta=(\zeta_{1},\dots,\zeta_{\ell}) is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-far from all responses yy, then there must be a point at which the blocks of ζ\zeta transition from being close to a response chain to not. Formally, there exists an index i∈[ℓ]i\in[\ell] such that the suffix (ζi+1,…,ζℓ)(\zeta_{i+1},\dots,\zeta_{\ell}) is close to some response, but (ζi,…,ζℓ)(\zeta_{i},\dots,\zeta_{\ell}) is not:

(∀(x,y)∈Π,𝖤𝖡𝖢[Φ,n](ζ,y)=0)\displaystyle\Big(\forall(x,y)\in\Pi,\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n](\zeta,y)=0\Big)
⊆⋁i∈[ℓ](𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i+1​(ζ,Π)∧¬𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ζ,Π)).\displaystyle\qquad\subseteq\bigvee_{i\in[\ell]}\Big(\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,i+1}(\zeta,\Pi)\;\wedge\;\neg\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,i}(\zeta,\Pi)\Big)\;.

This also covers the case when no suffix of ζ\zeta is close to a response chain. In particular, if no suffix of ζ\zeta is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-close to a response yy, then for all i∈[ℓ]i\in[\ell] we have 𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ζ,Π)=0\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,i}(\zeta,\Pi)=0, so ¬𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ζ,Π)=1\neg\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,i}(\zeta,\Pi)=1. Hence, the right-hand side still evaluates to 11 due to the i=ℓi=\ell clause, where 𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,ℓ+1​(ζ,Π)=1\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,\ell+1}(\zeta,\Pi)=1 is trivially true.

Now consider 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i} for i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, the event that there exists a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta such that the closeness chain of all-but-the-last block of ζ∗\zeta^{*} breaks exactly at index ii, yet 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖵𝖾𝗋r\mathsf{ChainVer}_{r} still accepts it. Formally,

𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄):=(∃ζ∗⪯ζ​ of length ​r​n​ such that𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖵𝖾𝗋r​(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗)=1,and ​𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i+1​((ζ1∗,…,ζr−1∗),Π),and ​¬𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​((ζ1∗,…,ζr−1∗),Π).).\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}):=\left(\begin{aligned} &\exists\,\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta\text{ of length }rn\text{ such that}\\ &\mathsf{ChainVer}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*})=1,\\ &\text{and }\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,i+1}((\zeta_{1}^{*},\ldots,\zeta_{r-1}^{*}),\Pi),\\ &\text{and }\neg\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain}_{\Phi,i}((\zeta_{1}^{*},\ldots,\zeta_{r-1}^{*}),\Pi).\end{aligned}\right). (3)

Lemma 6.3 shows that for any fixed i∈[r−1]i\in[r-1], this event occurs with probability at most negl⁡(λ)\mathrm{negl}(\lambda). Applying a union bound over all i∈[r−1]i\in[r-1] shows that the event ⋁i∈[r−1]𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)\bigvee_{i\in[r-1]}\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}) also occurs with negligible probability.

We conclude by showing that this suffices to prove unforgeability. Consider the event that an adversary successfully forges the watermark:

𝖵𝖾𝗋r(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=1∧(∀ζ′⪯ζ,(x,y)∈Π,|ζ′|≠(r−1)n∨𝖤𝖡𝖢[Φ,n](ζ′,y)=0).\mathsf{Ver}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=1\;\wedge\;\Big(\forall\,\zeta^{\prime}\preceq\zeta,(x,y)\in\Pi,\;|\zeta^{\prime}|\neq(r-1)n\;\vee\;\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n](\zeta^{\prime},y)=0\Big).

By definition of 𝖵𝖾𝗋r\mathsf{Ver}_{r}, if 𝖵𝖾𝗋r​(𝗏𝗄,ζ)=1\mathsf{Ver}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)=1, then there exists a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta of length r​nrn such that 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖵𝖾𝗋r​(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗)=1\mathsf{ChainVer}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*})=1. Moreover, if every (r−1)​n(r-1)n-sized substring ζ′⪯ζ\zeta^{\prime}\preceq\zeta is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-far from all responses, then the specific substring (ζ1∗,…,ζr−1∗)⪯ζ(\zeta_{1}^{*},\dots,\zeta_{r-1}^{*})\preceq\zeta, must be far from all responses. By the previous chain-breaking argument, this implies that there exists an index i∈[r−1]i\in[r-1] where the chain breaks. Hence, the event of a successful forgery implies the event ⋁i∈[r−1]𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)\bigvee_{i\in[r-1]}\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}), which we showed happens with negligible probability. ∎

Lemma 6.3.

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be a security parameter, let r=poly⁡(λ)r=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) satisfying r≥2r\geq 2 be any chain size, and let i∈[r−1]i\in[r-1] be any block index. Let (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖵𝖾𝗋r)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},\mathsf{Ver}_{r}) be the watermarking scheme presented in Figures 5 and 6. Under the same assumptions as Theorem 6.2, for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄,(𝖵𝖾𝗋r)𝗏𝗄:𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \zeta&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}},(\mathsf{Ver}_{r})_{\mathsf{vk}}}\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk})\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi is the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}) and 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}) is defined as in 3.

Proof.

Fix λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N}. The case i=r−1i=r-1 follows similarly to the proof of Theorem 6.1, therefore, we will prove the lemma for a fixed i∈[r−2]i\in[r-2]. Assume, toward contradiction, that there exists a polynomial q:ℕ→ℕq:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} such that

Pr⁡[𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)]≥1/q⁡(λ)\Pr[\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk})]\geq 1/q(\lambda)

Notice that the event 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}) implies the following event, specifically for the substring (ζi∗,ζi+1∗)(\zeta_{i}^{*},\zeta_{i+1}^{*}):

(∃ζ∗⪯ζ of size 2n such that 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖵𝖾𝗋(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ1∗,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖣𝖾𝖼(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,ζ2∗))=1,and ​∃(x,y)∈Π,t∈ℕ​ such that ​Φ​(ζ2∗,yt)=1​ and ​(Φ⁡(ζ1∗,yt−1)=0​ or ​t=1)).\left(\begin{aligned} &\exists\,\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta\text{ of size }2n\text{ such that }{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{Ver}\Big({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta_{1}^{*},{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},\zeta_{2}^{*})\Big)=1,\\ &\text{and }\exists(x,y)\in\Pi,t\in\mathbb{N}\text{ such that }\Phi(\zeta_{2}^{*},y_{t})=1\text{ and }\big(\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},y_{t-1})=0\text{ or }t=1\big)\end{aligned}\right).

Consequently, the event above occurs with probability at least 1/q⁡(λ)1/q(\lambda). Moreover, when this event occurs, the fact that Φ⁡(ζ2∗,yt)=1\Phi(\zeta_{2}^{*},y_{t})=1 and the block robustness of 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}} tell us that 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖣𝖾𝖼(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,ζ2∗){\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},\zeta_{2}^{*}) decodes to the message σt−1\sigma_{t-1} embedded in yty_{t} with all but negligible probability. Therefore, with inverse-polynomial probability, 𝒜\mathcal{A} finds a block ζ1∗∈{0,1}n\zeta_{1}^{*}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and a message σt−1∈{0,1}k\sigma_{t-1}\in\{0,1\}^{k} such that

(σt−1,yt)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌(𝒜𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄) and 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖵𝖾𝗋(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ1∗,σt−1)=1.(\sigma_{t-1},y_{t})\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Embed}}_{{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk}}})\text{ and }{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{Ver}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta_{1}^{*},\sigma_{t-1})=1\;.

By definition of 𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}, σt−1\sigma_{t-1} is either a uniformly random string when t=1t=1, or the robust signature of the previous block yt−1y_{t-1} when t>1t>1. We analyze these two cases separately.

  1. 1.

    σt−1←{0,1}k\sigma_{t-1}\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{k} is a uniformly random string, independent of ζ1∗\zeta_{1}^{*}. We have that

    𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖵𝖾𝗋(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ1∗,σt−1)=1{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{Ver}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\,\zeta_{1}^{*},\,\sigma_{t-1})=1

    with inverse-polynomial probability. But then, there exists an adversary ℬ𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝗌𝗄(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗏𝗄)\mathcal{B}^{{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{vk}) against the strong unforgeability of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}} that simulates 𝒜\mathcal{A} and outputs ζ1∗\zeta_{1}^{*}, along with a uniformly random string σ′←{0,1}k\sigma^{\prime}\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{k}. This verifies with inverse-polynomial probability, even though σ′\sigma^{\prime} is likely not any of the signatures seen by ℬ\mathcal{B}.

  2. 2.

    σt−1←𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄,yt−1)\sigma_{t-1}\leftarrow{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk},y_{t-1}) is a robust signature of the previous block. In this case,

    (yt−1,σt−1)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄).(y_{t-1},\sigma_{t-1})\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}_{{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk}}}). (4)

    However, we have that Φ⁡(ζ1∗,yt−1)=0\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},y_{t-1})=0. Either (ζ1∗,σt−1)(\zeta_{1}^{*},\sigma_{t-1}) contradicts the unforgeability of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}, or there exists a different message m≠yt−1m\neq y_{t-1} such that

    (m,σt−1)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄)​ and ​Φ​(ζ1∗,m)=1.(m,\sigma_{t-1})\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}_{{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk}}})\text{ and }\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},m)=1\;.

    This, however, breaks the unique signature property of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}, because the adversary finds two different messages m≠yt−1m\neq y_{t-1} with the same signature σt−1\sigma_{t-1}, where ζ1∗\zeta_{1}^{*} is Φ\Phi-far from yt−1y_{t-1} but Φ\Phi-close to mm. Thus, in the case, 𝒜\mathcal{A} either breaks unforgeability or unique signatures of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}.

In both cases, we obtain a contradiction to the security of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}. Therefore, 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)\mathsf{ChainForgery}_{i}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}) occurs only with negligible probability. ∎

6.3 Recoverable watermarking

If the robust signature scheme 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}} is recoverable, meaning it includes a recovery algorithm 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Rec}} that can reconstruct the original message from its signature and a perturbed version of that message, then we can recover the original prefix of the errored text using 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}}. Notably, 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} does not rely on the underlying language model QQ or generation prompt xx. Consequently, it enables users to recover original content using only the verification key and modified text. We obtain the following guarantees:

  • •

    (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],2​n,n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],2n,n)-robust recoverability: if an (adversarially chosen) ζ\zeta contains a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta of size r​nrn for some r≥2r\geq 2, where the blocks (ζ1∗,…,ζr∗)(\zeta^{*}_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{r}^{*}) are blockwise Φ\Phi-close to rr consecutive response blocks (yt,…,yt+r−1)(y_{t},\ldots,y_{t+r-1}), then 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ){\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta) will recover a substring of that response, ξ⪯y\xi\preceq y of size (r−1)​n(r-1)n. In particular, in our construction, ξ=(yt,…,yt+r−2)\xi=(y_{t},\ldots,y_{t+r-2}).

  • •

    (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],n)-unforgeable recoverability: if an (adversarially chosen) ζ\zeta leads to a recovery ξ∈𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)\xi\in{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta) then ξ\xi must satisfy:

    1. 1.

      ξ\xi has size r​nrn for some r≥1r\geq 1,

    2. 2.

      ξ\xi is a substring of some close response yy, i.e., ξ⪯y\xi\preceq y, and there exists ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta of size r​nrn that is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-close to yy.

    In particular, in our construction, ζ∗\zeta^{*} is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-close to ξ\xi and ξ\xi forms chain of blocks in yy.

Our recovery algorithm leverages the chaining idea from the previous section to not only reconstruct individual nn-bit blocks using 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}, but to also recover multi-block prefixes when the adversary has approximately copied a chain of consecutive watermarked blocks. The idea is to apply chain recoverability—analogous to chain verification—with every window size r​nrn, ensuring recovery from any long enough substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta with |ζ∗|≥2​n|\zeta^{*}|\geq 2n.

The subroutine 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼r\mathsf{ChainRec}_{r} takes in an rr-block chain and attempts to recover the first r−1r-1 blocks.

Corollary 6.4 (Recoverable watermarking).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter and let k,n=poly⁡(λ)k,n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be any message and block size, respectively. Let Φ\Phi be any closeness predicate, and QQ be any language model. Suppose that:

  • •

    𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀⁡[𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽,𝖣𝖾𝖼]{\mathsf{Steg}}[{\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Embed}},{\mathsf{Dec}}] is a message size kk, block size nn block steganography scheme for QQ with (secret or public key) Φ\Phi-robustness (Definition 4.11).

  • •

    𝖱𝖣𝖲⁡[𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇,𝖵𝖾𝗋]{\mathsf{RDS}}[{\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Sign}},\mathsf{Ver}] is a message size nn, signature size kk Φ\Phi-recoverable digital signature scheme (Definition 5.2) that has unique signatures w.r.t. Φ\Phi (Definition 5.3).

Then the construction (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) in Figures 5 and 7 is a recoverable watermarking scheme with (secret or public key) (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],2​n,n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],2n,n)-robustness and (secret or public key) (𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n],n)(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n],n)-unforgeability.

Proof.

Fix λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} and a PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Let

(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄)←𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ),(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄)←𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖦𝖾𝗇(1λ).({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda}),\quad({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\;.

Denote 𝗏𝗄=(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄)\mathsf{vk}=({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk}) and 𝗌𝗄=(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄)\mathsf{sk}=({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk},{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk}). Let ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄​(𝗏𝗄)\zeta\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}(\mathsf{vk}). We prove the public key version for both properties; the secret key version follow analogously.

Robust recoverability.

Suppose there exists a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta with |ζ∗|≥2​n|\zeta^{*}|\geq 2n and a pair (x,y)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄)(x,y)\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}) such that ζ∗\zeta^{*} and yy are close under 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]. Then there exist r,t∈ℕr,t\in\mathbb{N}, with r≥2r\geq 2, such that |ζ∗|=r​n|\zeta^{*}|=rn and

Φ⁡(ζj∗,yt+j−1)=1,∀j∈[r].\Phi(\zeta^{*}_{j},y_{t+j-1})=1,\;\forall j\in[r]\;.

Fix j∈[r−1]j\in[r-1]. As in the proof of robustness,

σj←𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖣𝖾𝖼(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,ζj+1∗)\sigma_{j}\leftarrow{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},\zeta_{j+1}^{*})

is the signature of yt+j−1y_{t+j-1} with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda). Since Φ⁡(ζj∗,yt+j−1)=1\Phi(\zeta^{*}_{j},y_{t+j-1})=1, the recovery algorithm of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}} satisfies 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖱𝖾𝖼(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζj∗,σj)=yt+j−1{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta_{j}^{*},\sigma_{j})=y_{t+j-1} with probability at least 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda) . Applying a union bound over all j∈[r−1]j\in[r-1], we conclude that

𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼r​(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗)=(yt,…,yt+r−2),\mathsf{ChainRec}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*})=(y_{t},\ldots,y_{t+r-2}),

which is a substring of yy of size |ζ∗|−n|\zeta^{*}|-n, with all but negligible probability. Since r≤⌊|ζ|/n⌋r\leq\lfloor|\zeta|/n\rfloor (otherwise r​n>|ζ|rn>|\zeta| and ζ∗\zeta^{*} could not be a substring of ζ\zeta), 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ){\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta) calls 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼r​(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗)\mathsf{ChainRec}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*}) during its execution, so the chain (yt,…,yt+r−2)(y_{t},\ldots,y_{t+r-2}), which is an (|ζ∗|−n)(|\zeta^{*}|-n)-sized substring of yy, will be added to the final output list with all but negligible probability.

Unforgeable recoverability.

The proof follows similarly to the proof of unforgeable chain verification. Let Π\Pi be the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}). For a predicate Φ\Phi and a block index i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}, define

𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖤𝗑𝖺𝖼𝗍𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ξ,Π):=(∃(x,y)∈Π,t∈ℕ​ such that ξj=yt+j−i,∀j∈{i,…,ℓ}).\mathsf{SuffixFormsExactChain}_{\Phi,i}(\xi,\Pi):=\left(\begin{aligned} &\exists(x,y)\in\Pi,t\in\mathbb{N}\text{ such that }\\ &\xi_{j}=y_{t+j-i},\;\forall j\in\{i,\ldots,\ell\}\end{aligned}\right).

the event that an input string ξ∈{0,1}∗\xi\in\{0,1\}^{*} forms an exact chain of blocks in some response yy (in contrast with 𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝖾𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇\mathsf{SuffixFormsCloseChain} 2 from the chain verification proof, which only required the input was close to a chain of blocks in some response yy). Moreover, define

𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ζ,ξ,Π):=(∃ℓ∈ℕ​ such that ​|ζ|=|ξ|=ℓ​n​ and(i>ℓ​ orCLOSE(𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]​((ζi,…,ζℓ),(ξi,…,ξℓ))=1CLOSEOPENOPENand ​𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖤𝗑𝖺𝖼𝗍𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ξ,Π)))).\mathsf{SuffixRecoversChain}_{\Phi,i}(\zeta,\xi,\Pi):=\left(\begin{aligned} &\exists\,\ell\in\mathbb{N}\text{ such that }|\zeta|=|\xi|=\ell n\text{ and}\\ &\Big(i>\ell\text{ or}\\ &\big(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]\big((\zeta_{i},\ldots,\zeta_{\ell}),\,(\xi_{i},\ldots,\xi_{\ell})\big)=1\\ &\text{and }\mathsf{SuffixFormsExactChain}_{\Phi,i}(\xi,\Pi)\big)\Big)\end{aligned}\right).

Given two sequences ζ,ξ∈{0,1}ℓ​n\zeta,\xi\in\{0,1\}^{\ell n} of ℓ\ell blocks of size nn, this event asserts that the suffix starting from the iith block (ζi,…,ζℓ)(\zeta_{i},\ldots,\zeta_{\ell}) is blockwise Φ\Phi-close to the blocks (ξi,…,ξℓ)(\xi_{i},\ldots,\xi_{\ell}), and that ξ\xi forms of chain of blocks in some response yy. When i=1i=1, this implies that ξ⪯y\xi\preceq y for some response yy and that ζ\zeta is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n] close to yy.

Now notice that if a string ζ=(ζ1,…,ζℓ)\zeta=(\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{\ell}) and recovery ξ=(ξ1,…,ξℓ)\xi=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{\ell}) do not form a recovery chain—that is, either ξ\xi does not form a chain of blocks in some response yy, or ζ\zeta is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-far from ξ\xi—then there must be some index i∈[ℓ]i\in[\ell] at which the chain transitions from being a valid recovery chain to not:

(𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]​(ζ,ξ)=0∨¬𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗆𝗌𝖤𝗑𝖺𝖼𝗍𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,1​(ξ,Π))\displaystyle\Big(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n](\zeta,\xi)=0\;\vee\;\neg\mathsf{SuffixFormsExactChain}_{\Phi,1}(\xi,\Pi)\Big)
⊆⋁i∈[ℓ](𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i+1​(ζ,ξ,Π)∧¬𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​(ζ,ξ,Π)).\displaystyle\qquad\subseteq\bigvee_{i\in[\ell]}\Big(\mathsf{SuffixRecoversChain}_{\Phi,i+1}(\zeta,\xi,\Pi)\;\wedge\;\neg\mathsf{SuffixRecoversChain}_{\Phi,i}(\zeta,\xi,\Pi)\Big)\;.

Now, for i,r∈ℕi,r\in\mathbb{N}, consider the event 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i,r\mathsf{ChainRecForgery}_{i,r}: there exists a substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta such that 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼r​(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗)\mathsf{ChainRec}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*}) successfully recovers some string ξ\xi, but for which the recovery chain between ζ∗\zeta^{*} and ξ\xi breaks at index ii. Formally,

𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i,r​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄):=(∃ζ∗⪯ζ​ of length ​r​n​ such that 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼r​(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗)=ξ​ with ⟂⋠ξ,and ​𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i+1​((ζ1∗,…,ζr−1∗),ξ,Π),and ​¬𝖲𝗎𝖿𝖿𝗂𝗑𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇Φ,i​((ζ1∗,…,ζr−1∗),ξ,Π)).\mathsf{ChainRecForgery}_{i,r}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}):=\left(\begin{aligned} &\exists\,\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta\text{ of length }rn\text{ such that }\\ &\mathsf{ChainRec}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*})=\xi\;\text{ with }\perp\not\preceq\xi,\\ &\text{and }\mathsf{SuffixRecoversChain}_{\Phi,i+1}((\zeta_{1}^{*},\ldots,\zeta_{r-1}^{*}),\xi,\Pi),\\ &\text{and }\neg\mathsf{SuffixRecoversChain}_{\Phi,i}((\zeta_{1}^{*},\ldots,\zeta_{r-1}^{*}),\xi,\Pi)\end{aligned}\right). (5)

Lemma 6.5 shows that for any fixed r=poly⁡(λ)r=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) with r≥2r\geq 2 and i∈[r−1]i\in[r-1], this event occurs with probability at most negl⁡(λ)\mathrm{negl}(\lambda). Applying a union bound over all r∈{2,…,⌊|ζ|/n⌋},i∈[r−1]r\in\{2,\ldots,\lfloor|\zeta|/n\rfloor\},i\in[r-1] shows that the event ⋁i,r𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i,r​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)\bigvee_{i,r}\mathsf{ChainRecForgery}_{i,r}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}) also occurs with negligible probability.

We conclude by showing that this suffices to prove unforgeable recoverability. Consider the event that an adversary successfully forges:

ξ∈𝖱𝖾𝖼(𝗏𝗄,ζ)∧(∀ζ′⪯ζ,(x,y)∈Π,|ζ′|≠|ξ|∨ξ⋠y∨𝖤𝖡𝖢[Φ,n](ζ′,y)=0).\xi\in{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta)\;\wedge\;\Big(\forall\,\zeta^{\prime}\preceq\zeta,(x,y)\in\Pi,\;|\zeta^{\prime}|\neq|\xi|\;\vee\;\xi\not\preceq y\;\vee\;\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n](\zeta^{\prime},y)=0\Big).

By definition of 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}}, if ξ∈𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄,ζ)\xi\in{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta), then there exists an r∈{2,…,⌊|ζ|/n⌋}r\in\{2,\ldots,\lfloor|\zeta|/n\rfloor\} and substring ζ∗⪯ζ\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta of size r​nrn where 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖵𝖾𝗋r​(𝗏𝗄,ζ∗)=ξ\mathsf{ChainVer}_{r}(\mathsf{vk},\zeta^{*})=\xi, ⟂⋠ξ\perp\not\preceq\xi, and |ξ|=(r−1)​n|\xi|=(r-1)n. Moreover, if for every |ξ||\xi|-sized substring ζ′⪯ζ\zeta^{\prime}\preceq\zeta and every response yy, either ξ⋠y\xi\not\preceq y or ζ′\zeta^{\prime} is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-far from yy, then either ζ′\zeta^{\prime} is 𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φ,n]\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi,n]-far from ξ\xi or ξ\xi does not form a chain in any response.

By the previous chain breaking argument, this means that the suffix recovery chain must break at some point for every substring ζ′\zeta^{\prime} of size |ξ||\xi|, including the specific substring (ζ1∗,…,ζr−1∗)(\zeta_{1}^{*},\ldots,\zeta_{r-1}^{*}). Hence, the event of a successful forgery implies the event ⋁i,r𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i,r​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)\bigvee_{i,r}\mathsf{ChainRecForgery}_{i,r}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}), which we showed happens with negligible probability. ∎

Lemma 6.5.

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be any security parameter, let r=poly⁡(λ)r=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) satisfying r≥2r\geq 2 be any chain size, and let i∈[r−1]i\in[r-1] be any block index. Let (𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖶𝖺𝗍,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Gen}},{\mathsf{Wat}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) be the watermarking scheme presented in Figures 5 and 7. Under the same assumptions as Corollary 6.4, for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr⁡[(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)ζ←𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄,𝖱𝖾𝖼𝗏𝗄:𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i,r​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)]≤negl⁡(λ),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Gen}}(1^{\lambda})\\ \zeta&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}},{\mathsf{Rec}}_{\mathsf{vk}}}\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\mathsf{ChainRecForgery}_{i,r}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk})\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;,

where Π\Pi is the transcript 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄){\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}}) and 𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i,r​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)\mathsf{ChainRecForgery}_{i,r}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk}) is defined as in 5.

Proof.

Fix λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N}. The case i=r−1i=r-1 is similar to the proof of Theorem 6.1, but by using the unforgeable recoverability of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}} instead of standard unforgeability. Hence, we prove the lemma for a fixed i∈[r−2]i\in[r-2]. Assume, toward contradiction, that there exists a polynomial q:ℕ→ℕq:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N} such that

Pr⁡[𝖢𝗁𝖺𝗂𝗇𝖱𝖾𝖼𝖥𝗈𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗋𝗒i,r​(ζ,Π,𝗏𝗄)]≥1/q⁡(λ).\Pr[\mathsf{ChainRecForgery}_{i,r}(\zeta,\Pi,\mathsf{vk})]\geq 1/q(\lambda)\;.

Notice that this event implies the following event, specifically for the substring (ζi∗,ζi+1∗)(\zeta_{i}^{*},\zeta_{i+1}^{*}):

(∃ζ∗⪯ζ​ of size ​2​n​ such that𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖱𝖾𝖼(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ1∗,𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖣𝖾𝖼(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,ζ2∗))=ξ∈{0,1}n,and ​∃(x,y)∈Π,t∈ℕ​ such thatΦ⁡(ζ2∗,yt)=1​ and ​(Φ⁡(ζ1∗,ξ)=0​ or ​ξ≠yt−1​ or ​t=1)).\left(\begin{aligned} &\exists\,\zeta^{*}\preceq\zeta\text{ of size }2n\text{ such that}\\ &{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}\Big({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta_{1}^{*},{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},\zeta_{2}^{*})\Big)=\xi\in\{0,1\}^{n},\\ &\text{and }\exists(x,y)\in\Pi,t\in\mathbb{N}\text{ such that}\\ \ &\Phi(\zeta_{2}^{*},y_{t})=1\text{ and }\Big(\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},\xi)=0\text{ or }\xi\neq y_{t-1}\text{ or }t=1\Big)\end{aligned}\right). (6)

Consequently, the event above occurs with probability at least 1/q⁡(λ)1/q(\lambda). Moreover, when this event occurs, the fact that Φ⁡(ζ2∗,yt)=1\Phi(\zeta_{2}^{*},y_{t})=1 and the block-robustness of 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀{\mathsf{Steg}} tell us that 𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖣𝖾𝖼(𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗏𝗄,ζ2∗){\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Dec}}({\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{vk},\zeta_{2}^{*}) decodes to the message encoded in yty_{t} with all but negligible probability. Therefore, with inverse-polynomial probability, 𝒜\mathcal{A} finds a block ζ1∗∈{0,1}n\zeta_{1}^{*}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and a message σt−1∈{0,1}k\sigma_{t-1}\in\{0,1\}^{k} such that

(σt−1,yt)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌(𝒜𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝖤𝗆𝖻𝖾𝖽𝖲𝗍𝖾𝗀.𝗌𝗄) and 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖱𝖾𝖼(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ1∗,σt−1)=ξ∈{0,1}n.(\sigma_{t-1},y_{t})\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{Steg}}.{\mathsf{Embed}}_{{\mathsf{Steg}}.\mathsf{sk}}})\text{ and }{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta_{1}^{*},\sigma_{t-1})=\xi\in\{0,1\}^{n}\;.

By definition of 𝖶𝖺𝗍𝗌𝗄{\mathsf{Wat}}_{\mathsf{sk}}, the value σt−1\sigma_{t-1} is either a uniformly random string when t=1t=1, or the robust signature of the previous block yt−1y_{t-1} when t>1t>1. We analyze these two cases separately.

  1. 1.

    σt−1←{0,1}k\sigma_{t-1}\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{k} is a uniformly random string. We have that

    𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖱𝖾𝖼(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ1∗,σt−1)≠⟂{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\,\zeta_{1}^{*},\,\sigma_{t-1})\neq\perp

    with inverse-polynomial probability. As in the proof of chain verification, there exists an adversary against the unforgeable recovery of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}.

  2. 2.

    σt−1←𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,yt−1)\sigma_{t-1}\leftarrow{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},y_{t-1}) is a robust signature of the previous block. In this case,

    (yt−1,σt−1)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄).(y_{t-1},\sigma_{t-1})\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}_{{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk}}})\;.

    Since 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖱𝖾𝖼(𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄,ζ1∗,σt−1)=ξ∈{0,1}n{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}({\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk},\zeta_{1}^{*},\sigma_{t-1})=\xi\in\{0,1\}^{n}, it must be that

    (ξ,σt−1)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗉𝗄)​ and ​Φ​(ζ1∗,ξ)=1.(\xi,\sigma_{t-1})\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}_{{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{pk}}})\text{ and }\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},\xi)=1\;. (7)

    with all but negligible probability; otherwise, 𝒜\mathcal{A} would break the unforgeable recoverability of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}. Therefore, we may further condition on this event.

    Together event 6, which guarantees that either Φ⁡(ζ1∗,yt−1)=0\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},y_{t-1})=0 or ξ≠yt−1\xi\neq y_{t-1}, and event 7, which guarantees that Φ⁡(ζ1∗,ξ)=1\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},\xi)=1, imply that ξ≠yt−1\xi\neq y_{t-1}; otherwise, ζ1∗\zeta_{1}^{*} would be simultaneously Φ\Phi-close to and Φ\Phi-far from ξ\xi, a contradiction.

    When ξ≠yt−1\xi\neq y_{t-1}, we have two subcases:

    1. (a)

      If Φ⁡(ζ1∗,yt−1)=1\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},y_{t-1})=1, then with inverse-polynomial probability, 𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(𝗏𝗄CLOSE,{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Rec}}(\mathsf{vk}, OPENζ1∗,σt−1)≠yt−1\zeta_{1}^{*},\sigma_{t-1})\neq y_{t-1} despite the fact that (yt−1,σt−1)∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌⁡(𝒜𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝖲𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖱𝖣𝖲.𝗌𝗄)(y_{t-1},\sigma_{t-1})\in{\mathsf{Trans}}(\mathcal{A}^{{\mathsf{RDS}}.{\mathsf{Sign}}_{{\mathsf{RDS}}.\mathsf{sk}}}) and Φ⁡(ζ1∗,yt−1)=1\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},y_{t-1})=1. This contradicts the robust recoverability of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}.

    2. (b)

      If Φ⁡(ζ1∗,yt−1)=0\Phi(\zeta_{1}^{*},y_{t-1})=0, then 𝒜\mathcal{A} produces (ζ1∗,ξ,yt−1)(\zeta_{1}^{*},\xi,y_{t-1}) that violates the unique signature property of 𝖱𝖣𝖲{\mathsf{RDS}}.

In both cases, we arrive at a contradiction, proving that the scheme is in fact unforgeably recoverable. ∎

6.4 Instantiating Hamming watermarks

We instantiate our watermarking scheme for high-entropy language models. In particular, we combine our RDS construction (Corollary 5.11) with an existing secret key block steganography scheme (Theorem 4.14) to obtain a watermark that is secret key recoverable, robust, and unforgeable in the presence of a constant fraction of Hamming errors.

Corollary 6.6 (Concrete secret-key watermarking).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and suppose there exists

  • •

    A CRHF with output size m=m⁡(λ)m=m(\lambda).

  • •

    A strongly unforgeable digital signature with signature size k=k⁡(λ)k=k(\lambda).

  • •

    An ideal PRC with with error rate δ𝖯𝖱𝖢∈(0,14)\delta_{{\mathsf{PRC}}}\in(0,\frac{1}{4}) and information rate ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1)1313 13 Recall that for any error-rate δ𝖯𝖱𝖢∈(0,1/4)\delta_{{\mathsf{PRC}}}\in(0,1/4), there exists an ideal PRC with constant rate ρ=Ω⁡(1)\rho=\Omega(1), assuming subexponential hardness of LPN [4, Theorem 3]..

Let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) such that n≥λn\geq\lambda and (m+k)/n=o⁡(1)(m+k)/n=o(1) be the block size. Let ϵ<δ𝖯𝖱𝖢\epsilon<\delta_{{\mathsf{PRC}}} be any constant and let QQ be any language model satisfying the following entropy condition,

∀π∈{0,1}∗,y←Q¯n​(π)​ satisfies ​H∞​(y)≥4​(12−ϵ)​n.\forall\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*},y\leftarrow{\overline{Q}}_{n}(\pi)\text{ satisfies }H_{\infty}(y)\geq 4\Big(\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon}\Big)n\;.

Let δ>0\delta>0 be any constant such that

δ<min⁡{δ𝖱𝖣𝖲​(ρ),δ𝖯𝖱𝖢−ϵ},\displaystyle\delta<\min\left\{\delta_{{\mathsf{RDS}}}(\rho),\delta_{{\mathsf{PRC}}}-\epsilon\right\}\;,

where δ𝖱𝖣𝖲​(ρ):=sup{δ∈(0,1/2)∣ρ>H2𝖡𝖹​(δ)}\delta_{{\mathsf{RDS}}}(\rho):=\sup\{\delta\in(0,1/2)\mid\rho>H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta)\}. Then, our construction in Corollary 6.4 yields a secret key

(𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[𝖧𝖺𝗆δ,n],2​n)​-robust and ​(𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[𝖧𝖺𝗆δ,n],n)​-unforgeable\big(\mathsf{EBC}[{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta},n],2n\big)\text{-robust and }\big(\mathsf{EBC}[{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta},n],n\big)\text{-unforgeable}

recoverable watermarking scheme for QQ.

Proof.

From the ideal PRC assumption and Theorem 4.14, for any error rate δ≤δ𝖯𝖱𝖢−ϵ\delta\leq\delta_{{\mathsf{PRC}}}-\epsilon, there exists a block steganography scheme for QQ with block size nn, message size ρ​n\rho n. From the CRHF and strongly unforgeable digital signature assumptions and Corollary 5.11, for any δ≤δ𝖱𝖣𝖲​(ρ)\delta\leq\delta_{{\mathsf{RDS}}}(\rho), there exists a 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}-recoverable digital signature scheme with message size nn and signature size ρ​n+o⁡(n)\rho n+o(n). We apply Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.4 to get the result. Note that the block steganography message size and the digital signature size differ by o⁡(n)o(n). Our proof ignores this difference, but it could be made exact by assuming an ideal PRC with a slightly better information rate ρ′>ρ\rho^{\prime}>\rho. ∎

Moreover, we leverage an existing public-key block steganography scheme (Theorem 4.16) to obtain a public-key construction that is robust to a subconstant fraction of Hamming errors, subject to the restriction that the first ℓ\ell bits of each block are error-free, as captured by the predicate Φδ\Phi_{\delta} defined in Theorem 4.16.

Corollary 6.7 (Concrete public-key watermarking).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and suppose there exists

  • •

    A CRHF with output size m=m⁡(λ)m=m(\lambda).

  • •

    A strongly unforgeable digital signature with signature size k=k⁡(λ)k=k(\lambda).

Let QQ be any language model such that for some ℓ=poly⁡(λ)\ell=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda),

∀π∈{0,1}∗,y←Q¯ℓ​(π)​ satisfies ​H∞​(y)≥ω⁡(log⁡λ).\forall\pi\in\{0,1\}^{*},y\leftarrow{\overline{Q}}_{\ell}(\pi)\text{ satisfies }H_{\infty}(y)\geq\omega(\log\lambda)\;.

Let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) be any block size satisfying ℓ⁡(m+k)/n=o⁡(1)\ell(m+k)/n=o(1). There exists a subconstant δmax=Θ⁡(1ℓ​log⁡n)\delta_{\mathrm{max}}=\Theta(\frac{1}{\ell\log n}) such that for any δ=o⁡(1)\delta=o(1) satisfying δ⁡(λ)≤δmax​(λ)​∀λ∈ℕ\delta(\lambda)\leq\delta_{\mathrm{max}}(\lambda)\;\forall\lambda\in\mathbb{N}, there exists a public key

(𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[Φδ,n],2​n)​-robust and ​(𝖤𝖡𝖢⁡[𝖧𝖺𝗆δ,n],n)​-unforgeable\big(\mathsf{EBC}[\Phi_{\delta},n],2n\big)\text{-robust and }\big(\mathsf{EBC}[{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta},n],n\big)\text{-unforgeable}

recoverable watermarking scheme for QQ in the random oracle model, where Φδ\Phi_{\delta} is defined the same as in Theorem 4.16.

Proof.

Fix λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} sufficiently large. By Theorem 4.16, in the random oracle model there exist constants ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and δ∗∈(0,1/2)\delta^{*}\in(0,1/2) such that for any δ≤δ∗\delta\leq\delta^{*}, there exists a public key Φδ\Phi_{\delta}-robust block steganography scheme for QQ with block size nn and message size ρ⁡(n/ℓ−1)\rho(n/\ell-1).

Moreover, the CRHF and strongly unforgeable digital signature assumptions, Corollary 5.13 guarantees that for any δ=o⁡(1)\delta=o(1), there exists a 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}-robust digital signature scheme with signature size

O⁡(δ​n​log⁡n)+m+k≤C​δ​n​log⁡n+o⁡(n/ℓ)O(\delta n\log n)+m+k\leq C\delta n\log n+o(n/\ell)

for some constant C>0C>0.

To apply our main theorem, we require that the signature fits as a message for the block steganography scheme:

C​δ​n​log⁡n+o⁡(n/ℓ)≤ρ⁡(n/ℓ−1).C\delta n\log n+o(n/\ell)\leq\rho(n/\ell-1)\;.

This condition holds whenever

δ⁡(λ)≤δmax​(λ)​ where ​δmax=ρ⁡(n/ℓ)−ρ−o⁡(n/ℓ)C​n​log⁡n=Θ⁡(1ℓ​log⁡n)\delta(\lambda)\leq\delta_{\mathrm{max}}(\lambda)\text{ where }\delta_{\mathrm{max}}=\frac{\rho(n/\ell)-\rho-o(n/\ell)}{Cn\log n}=\Theta(\frac{1}{\ell\log n})\;

Therefore, there exists a 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ⁡(λ){\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta(\lambda)}-recoverable signature scheme with message size nn and signature size at most ρ⁡(n/ℓ−1)\rho(n/\ell-1). Note we can adjust δmax\delta_{\mathrm{max}} so that additionally, δ⁡(λ)≤δ∗\delta(\lambda)\leq\delta^{*} for all λ\lambda, since δ∗\delta^{*} is constant. Then both a Φδ\Phi_{\delta}-robust block steganography scheme and a 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}-recoverable signature scheme exist.

Furthermore, for any strings y,y′∈{0,1}∗y,y^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{*}, we have

Φδ​(y,y′)=1⟹𝖧𝖺𝗆δ​(y,y′)=1,\Phi_{\delta}(y,y^{\prime})=1\implies{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta}(y,y^{\prime})=1,

because if at most δ⁡(nℓ−1)\delta\big(\frac{n}{\ell}-1\big) blocks of size ℓ\ell differ between inputs yy and y′y^{\prime}, then at most δ⁡(n−ℓ)≤δ​n\delta(n-\ell)\leq\delta n bits differ. It follows that the robust signature is also Φδ\Phi_{\delta}-robustly recoverable. Applying Theorem 6.1 with these constructions then yields the desired result. ∎

Appendix A Strong Difference Recovery and Homomorphic PPH

We notice that the PPH construction of Holmgren et al. [26], when instantiated with a homomorphic collision-resistant hash function (CRHF), satisfies two notable properties: it supports strong difference recovery and it is homomorphic. We formalize both properties and state the guarantees.

Note, however, that our recoverable watermarking scheme does not rely on strong recovering or homomorphic PPHs, as the perturbed input x′x^{\prime} is available in the clear. Instead, the notion of sharp sketches, introduced in Section B, more accurately captures the relevant functionality. We include strong difference recovery and homomorphic PPHs here primarily for completeness.

Definition A.1 (Strong difference recovering PPH).

A Φ\Phi-PPH (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁,𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅)({\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Hash}},{\mathsf{Eval}}) is strong difference-recovering if there exists a PPT algorithm 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} such that for any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr⁡[h←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)(x,x′)←𝒜⁡(1λ,h)Δ←𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(h,h⁡(x),h⁡(x′)):(Δ≠x⊕x′∧Φ⁡(x,x′)=1)∨(Δ≠⊥∧Φ(x,x′)=0)]≤negl⁡(λ)\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}h&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (x,x^{\prime})&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(1^{\lambda},h)\\ \Delta&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Rec}}(h,h(x),h(x^{\prime}))\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\big(\Delta\neq x\oplus x^{\prime}\wedge\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=1\big)\\ \vee\;\big(\Delta\neq\bot\wedge\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=0\big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)
Definition A.2 (Homomorphic PPH).

A PPH scheme (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁,𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅)({\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Hash}},{\mathsf{Eval}}) with input size nn and hash size kk is said to be homomorphic if there exists a fixed abelian group (𝒢n,+)(\mathcal{G}_{n},+) and an injective map ψ:𝒢n→{0,1}k\psi:\mathcal{G}_{n}\to\{0,1\}^{k} such that for every hash function representation h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}, there exists an efficiently computable1414 14 That is, computable using poly⁡(n)\mathrm{poly}(n) many elementary algebraic operations. homomorphism φ:ℤn→𝒢n\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^{n}\to\mathcal{G}_{n} satisfying

𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(h,x)=ψ⁡(φ⁡(x))for all ​x∈{0,1}n.\displaystyle{\mathsf{Hash}}(h,x)=\psi(\varphi(x))\quad\text{for all }x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\;.

In other words, every hash function h:{0,1}n→{0,1}kh:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{k} in the family ℋ\mathcal{H} can be expressed as the composition of a homomorphism φ:ℤn→𝒢n\varphi:\mathbb{Z}^{n}\to\mathcal{G}_{n} and a fixed injective embedding ψ:𝒢n→{0,1}k\psi:\mathcal{G}_{n}\to\{0,1\}^{k}.

Notation for homomorphic PPH.

If 𝖯𝖯𝖧⁡[𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁,𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅]{\mathsf{PPH}}[{\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Hash}},{\mathsf{Eval}}] is homomorphic, we abuse notation and write h⁡(x)−h⁡(x′)=h⁡(x−x′)h(x)-h(x^{\prime})=h(x-x^{\prime}) for any h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} and x,x′∈{0,1}nx,x^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, where subtraction is interpreted over ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} (so that x−x′∈{−1,0,1}nx-x^{\prime}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{n}) and h⁡(x)h(x) refers to the group element φ⁡(x)∈𝒢n\varphi(x)\in\mathcal{G}_{n} (i.e., before applying the embedding ψ\psi into {0,1}k\{0,1\}^{k}).

Definition A.3 (Sparsity testing).

A homomorphic PPH scheme (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁,𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅)({\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Hash}},{\mathsf{Eval}}) is said to support sparsity testing if there exists an algorithm 𝖲𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅\mathsf{SparseEval} such that for all h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} and x,x′∈{0,1}nx,x^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{n},

𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(x),h⁡(x′))\displaystyle{\mathsf{Eval}}(h,h(x),h(x^{\prime})) =𝖲𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(x)−h⁡(x′))\displaystyle=\mathsf{SparseEval}(h,h(x)-h(x^{\prime}))
=𝖲𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅⁡(h,h⁡(Δ)),\displaystyle=\mathsf{SparseEval}(h,h(\Delta))\;,

where Δ=x−x′∈{−1,0,1}n\Delta=x-x^{\prime}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{n}, and the final equality follows from the homomorphic property.

In other words, if a homomorphic PPH supports sparsity testing, then its evaluation algorithm 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{Eval}} depends only on the hash function hh and the difference h⁡(x)−h⁡(x′)=h⁡(x−x′)h(x)-h(x^{\prime})=h(x-x^{\prime}), rather than on the individual hash values. Specifically, 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅{\mathsf{Eval}} returns 11 if the difference Δ\Delta is sparse, and 00 otherwise.

Holmgren et al.’s homomorphic PPH goes further by supporting sparse recovery: if Δ\Delta is sparse, then given only (h,h⁡(Δ))(h,h(\Delta)), their recovery algorithm 𝖱𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{Rec}} outputs Δ∈{−1,0,1}n\Delta\in\{-1,0,1\}^{n} exactly. Note that this recovers only the difference vector, not the preimages xx or x′x^{\prime}.

Theorem A.4 ([26, Corollary 6.7]).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and let n=poly⁡(λ)n=\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) denote the input size. Suppose there exists a homomorphic CRHF with output size ℓ=ℓ⁡(λ)\ell=\ell(\lambda) that is collision-resistant over {−1,0,1}n\{-1,0,1\}^{n} [26, Definition 6.1]. Then, for any constants δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and ρ>H3𝖡𝖹​(δ)⋅log2⁡3\rho>H_{3}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta)\cdot\log_{2}3, where H3𝖡𝖹​(⋅)H_{3}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\cdot) refers to the Blokh-Zyablov bound [26, Fact 2.12], there exists a strongly recoverable homomorphic PPH over the input domain {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} for 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta} with hash size ρ⋅n+ℓ\rho\cdot n+\ell.

Appendix B Sharp Sketches and Lower Bounds

A sharp sketch is a cryptographic primitive that enables efficient recovery given auxiliary input x′x^{\prime} in the clear. The goal is to reconstruct an input xx from its sketch g⁡(x)g(x) and a candidate x′x^{\prime} that is sufficiently close to it. Its defining feature is sharpness: 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(g,g⁡(x),x′){\mathsf{Rec}}(g,g(x),x^{\prime}) must output ⊥\bot if x′x^{\prime} is far from xx.

This notion is inspired by the secure sketches of Dodis et al. [16], but differs in both purpose and security guarantees. Secure sketches require unconditional hardness of inversion: it must be hard to recover xx from its sketch g⁡(x)g(x), even for an unbounded adversary. This necessitates a non-trivial compression rate ρ=k/n\rho=k/n, so secure sketches are compressive by definition. Their recoverability guarantee is also unconditional, requiring recovery to succeed for every x′x^{\prime} that is close to xx.

In contrast, sharp sketches enforce a different notion of security, one not centered on inversion. They require that no computationally-bounded adversary can produce input pairs (x,x′)(x,x^{\prime}) that violate the sharp recoverability condition (see Definition B.1). Thus, compressiveness is not required by definition. Even the identity sketch g⁡(x)=xg(x)=x qualifies as a (trivial) sharp sketch, though it would not qualify as a secure sketch. On the other hand, any secure sketch can be converted into a sharp sketch by returning ⊥\bot whenever x^=𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(g,g⁡(x),x′)\hat{x}={\mathsf{Rec}}(g,g(x),x^{\prime}) is either inconsistent g⁡(x)≠g⁡(x^)g(x)\neq g(\hat{x}) or far from x′x^{\prime}.

Sharp sketch constructions for Hamming predicates were given by Dodis et al. [16, Section 8.3]. We include it here for completeness and to enable precise reference in our watermarking scheme, where it plays a key role. Our main technical contribution is a generalization of the lower bound by Holmgren et al. [26], extending it from Hamming predicates to any predicate Φ\Phi that satisfies an efficient sampleability condition (Theorem B.5). When specialized to the Hamming case, our bound implies that the construction of Dodis et al. achieves nearly optimal sketch size, since the gap between the Hamming bound H⁡(δ)H(\delta) and the Blokh-Zyablov bound H2𝖡𝖹​(δ)H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta) is small (see also Remark 4.8). This shows that the recoverable digital signature in Corollary 5.11 is nearly optimal compared to constructions based on the generic PPH/sharp sketch transformation of Section 5.2.

Definition B.1 (Sharp sketch).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, let Φ\Phi be any predicate, and let n=n⁡(λ)n=n(\lambda) and k=k⁡(λ)k=k(\lambda) be such that k≤nk\leq n. A sharp sketching scheme for Φ\Phi with input size nn and sketch size kk is a triple of PPT algorithms (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖲𝗄𝖾𝗍𝖼𝗁,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Sketch}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) defined as follows:

  • •

    𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ){\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda}): samples a sketching function gg from a family of functions 𝒢λ\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}.

  • •

    𝖲𝗄𝖾𝗍𝖼𝗁⁡(g,x){\mathsf{Sketch}}(g,x): takes in x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} and outputs its sketch g⁡(x)∈{0,1}kg(x)\in\{0,1\}^{k}.

  • •

    𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(g,z,x′){\mathsf{Rec}}(g,z,x^{\prime}): takes in z∈{0,1}kz\in\{0,1\}^{k} and x′∈{0,1}nx^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, and returns an output in {0,1}n∪{⊥}\{0,1\}^{n}\cup\{\bot\}.

The scheme satisfies the following security guarantee:

Sharp recoverability: For any PPT adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A},

Pr⁡[g←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ);(x,x′)←𝒜⁡(1λ,g):(𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(g,g⁡(x),x′)≠x∧Φ⁡(x,x′)=1)∨(𝖱𝖾𝖼(g,g(x),x′)≠⊥∧Φ(x,x′)=0)]≤negl⁡(λ).\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}g&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda});\\ (x,x^{\prime})&\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(1^{\lambda},g)\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}\big({\mathsf{Rec}}(g,g(x),x^{\prime})\neq x\;\wedge\;\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=1\big)\\ \vee\;\big({\mathsf{Rec}}(g,g(x),x^{\prime})\neq\bot\;\wedge\;\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=0\big)\end{array}\right]\leq\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;.

We restate Theorem 5.6, which gave a difference recovery hash family for Hamming from CRHFs, in the language of sharp sketches.

Theorem B.2 (Sharp sketch for Hamming, adapted from [16, Section 8.3]).

Let λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} be the security parameter, and let n=n⁡(λ)n=n(\lambda) denote the input size. Suppose there exists a CRHF with output size ℓ=ℓ⁡(λ)\ell=\ell(\lambda). For any constants δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2) and ρ>H2𝖡𝖹​(δ)\rho>H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\delta), where H2𝖡𝖹​(⋅)H_{2}^{\mathsf{BZ}}(\cdot) refers to the Blokh-Zyablov bound, there exists a sharp sketching scheme (𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾,𝖲𝗄𝖾𝗍𝖼𝗁,𝖱𝖾𝖼)({\mathsf{Sample}},{\mathsf{Sketch}},{\mathsf{Rec}}) over {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} for 𝖧𝖺𝗆δ{\mathsf{Ham}}_{\delta} with sketch size ρ⋅n+ℓ\rho\cdot n+\ell.

Remark B.3 (PPH and sharp sketch).

By Proposition 5.5, every Hamming PPH yields a sharp sketch for the same predicate. However, the converse does not hold. For instance, the sharp sketching scheme in Theorem 5.6 does not give rise to a Hamming PPH, as it crucially relies on receiving x′x^{\prime} in the clear, rather than just its sketch. Note, however, that our recoverable digital signature algorithm (Section 5.3) does receive one input in the clear, and therefore sharp sketches suffice.

Lemma B.4 ([16], Lemma 2.2).

For random variables X,Y,ZX,Y,Z, where YY is supported over a set of size kk, we have

H∞​(X|Y,Z)≥H∞​(X|Z)−log⁡kH_{\infty}(X|Y,Z)\geq H_{\infty}(X|Z)-\log k
Theorem B.5 (Sharp sketch lower bound).

Let Φ\Phi any predicate and let A⊆{(x,x′)∈{0,1}n×{0,1}n:Φ⁡(x,x′)=1}A\subseteq\{(x,x^{\prime})\in\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{n}:\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=1\} be such that the uniform distribution 𝒰\mathcal{U} over pairs (x,x′)(x,x^{\prime}) conditioned on AA is efficiently sampleable. Then the sketch size of any sharp sketch for Φ\Phi is at least

n+log⁡𝒰⁡(A).\displaystyle n+\log\mathcal{U}(A)\;.
Proof.

Let XX be uniformly distributed over {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}, and let g:{0,1}n→{0,1}kg:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{k} be a sharp sketch drawn independently of XX. Then the min-entropy of XX conditioned on hh and g⁡(X)g(X), which we denote by H∞​(X∣h,g​(X))H_{\infty}(X\mid h,g(X)), satisfies:

H∞​(X∣g,g⁡(X))≥H∞​(X∣g)−k≥n−k.\displaystyle H_{\infty}(X\mid g,g(X))\geq H_{\infty}(X\mid g)-k\geq n-k\;.

In particular, no (even unbounded) adversary can “invert” (g,g⁡(X))(g,g(X)) to recover the original input XX with probability greater than 2−(n−k)2^{-(n-k)} when XX is drawn uniformly from {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}.

Now consider the following inversion strategy based on 𝖱𝖾𝖼(g,g(x),⋅){\mathsf{Rec}}(g,g(x),\cdot). Define a randomized algorithm 𝖨𝗇𝗏{\mathsf{Inv}} that, on input (g,g⁡(x))(g,g(x)), samples a fresh x′←{0,1}nx^{\prime}\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{n} and outputs 𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(g,g⁡(x),x′){\mathsf{Rec}}(g,g(x),x^{\prime}). Let μ\mu be the distribution of (x,x′)(x,x^{\prime}) sampled uniformly from {0,1}2​n\{0,1\}^{2n} conditioned on the event AA. By assumption, (x,x′)∈A(x,x^{\prime})\in A implies Φ⁡(x,x′)=1\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=1. Since μ\mu is efficiently sampleable and Φ⁡(x,x′)=1\Phi(x,x^{\prime})=1, guarantees of the sharp sketch gg yield

Pr[g←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)(x,x′)←μ:𝖱𝖾𝖼(g,g(x),x′)=x]≥1−negl(λ).\displaystyle\Pr\left[\begin{array}[]{rl}g&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (x,x^{\prime})&\leftarrow\mu\end{array}:{\mathsf{Rec}}(g,g(x),x^{\prime})=x\right]\geq 1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)\;.

Using the above recovery guarantee, we lower bound the success probability of 𝖨𝗇𝗏{\mathsf{Inv}} as follows.

Pr\displaystyle\Pr [g←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)x←{0,1}n:𝖨𝗇𝗏(g,g(x))=x]\displaystyle\bigg[\begin{array}[]{rl}g&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda})\\ x&\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\end{array}:\;{\mathsf{Inv}}(g,g(x))=x\bigg]
≥Pr⁡[g←𝖲𝖺𝗆𝗉𝗅𝖾⁡(1λ)(x,x′)←{0,1}2​n:𝖱𝖾𝖼⁡(g,g⁡(x),x′)=x|A]⋅𝒰⁡(A)\displaystyle\geq\Pr\bigg[\begin{array}[]{rl}g&\leftarrow{\mathsf{Sample}}(1^{\lambda})\\ (x,x^{\prime})&\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{2n}\end{array}:\begin{array}[]{rl}{\mathsf{Rec}}(g,g(x),x^{\prime})=x\;\bigg|\;A\end{array}\bigg]\cdot\mathcal{U}(A)
≥(1−negl⁡(λ))⋅𝒰⁡(A).\displaystyle\geq(1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda))\cdot\mathcal{U}(A)\;.

But from the earlier information-theoretic bound, no function gg with output size kk can support inversion with success probability greater than 2−(n−k)2^{-(n-k)}. Hence, we conclude

2−(n−k)≥𝒰⁡(A)⋅(1−negl⁡(λ)),\displaystyle 2^{-(n-k)}\geq\mathcal{U}(A)\cdot(1-\mathrm{negl}(\lambda))\;,

For sufficiently large λ\lambda, we have negl⁡(λ)<1/2\mathrm{negl}(\lambda)<1/2, which implies

k≥n+log⁡𝒰⁡(A).\displaystyle k\geq n+\log\mathcal{U}(A)\;.

∎

Claim B.6.

Let r=r⁡(n)r=r(n) be any efficiently computable function. Then, the uniform distribution 𝒰\mathcal{U} over pairs (x,x′)∈{0,1}n×{0,1}n(x,x^{\prime})\in\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{n} conditioned on ‖x−x′‖0=r\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{0}=r is efficiently sampleable.

Proof.

First, sample x←{0,1}nx\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{n} uniformly at random. Then sample an rr-sparse perturbation vector Δ∈{0,1}n\Delta\in\{0,1\}^{n} independently of xx. Finally, set x′=x⊕Δx^{\prime}=x\oplus\Delta. ∎

Corollary B.7.

Let r=r⁡(n)r=r(n) be any efficiently computable function. Then, for all sufficiently large nn, the sketch size of any sharp sketching scheme for 𝖧𝖺𝗆r/n{\mathsf{Ham}}_{r/n} is at least log⁡(nr)\log\binom{n}{r}.
